POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Sun, 08 Nov 2026 19:39:52 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 Wirecard fugitive claimed he toppled Sebastian Kurz in messages to Russian spy https://www.politico.eu/article/wirecard-fugitive-jan-marsalek-claimed-he-toppled-sebastian-kurz-in-messages-to-russian-spy/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 08 Nov 2026 16:57:23 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9290265 Jan Marsalek, the fugitive former Wirecard executive suspected by multiple countries of spying for Russia, claimed that he had helped to bring down Austrian Chancellor Sebastian Kurz, according to documents obtained by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, of which POLITICO is a part. 

Marsalek said he had been involved in an operation that had “successfully toppled” Kurz, who stepped down amid corruption allegations in 2021. 

The messages, detailed in investigation files seen by the Telegraph and the Global Reporters Network, were sent to Orlin Roussev, a spy-ring leader who received instructions from Marsalek and has since been jailed in Britain for espionage. The documents contain no independent evidence of the role Marsalek says he has played in Kurz’s downfall. 

If substantiated, Marsalek’s claims would be a clear indicator of the Russian state interfering directly in the political leadership of an EU country. The Kremlin has long sought to sow division and destabilize governments across Europe, according to assessments by multiple security agencies. 

Marsalek is one of the world’s most wanted men and has been on the run since June 2020 when his company, German tech giant Wirecard, collapsed with a €1.9 billion hole in its books.

Since his escape, he has been accused of working for the Kremlin for more than a decade while British police say he is involved in espionage on an “industrial” scale. He is wanted for fraud and is being investigated for spying in several European countries, including his native Austria.

Kurz was the world’s youngest leader when he first became chancellor of Austria in 2017 at the age of 31. But his stratospheric rise, which saw him hold the post twice, was marred by corruption allegations, including that public money was used for political advertising on his behalf. 

When members of Marsalek’s spy ring, led by Roussev, were arrested in the U.K., police seized hundreds of thousands of messages detailing operations plotted from British soil.

Some of these messages were shared with authorities, including Austrian officials, who are currently investigating whether their spies provided information to Marsalek and, in turn, to Russia.

‘Messy story’

One of the investigative files, examined by the Global Reporters Network, contains messages sent by a man whom authorities have identified as Marsalek, using the alias “Rupert Ticz,” on October 22, 2021.

Marsalek mentions a “guy” who “was actually working for us for a while,” adding: “now he’s the victim of a witch-hunt by the team of the former chancellor.”

He goes on to say that “we’ve successfully toppled” the former chancellor “by confiscating the mobile phone” of a friend of the then chancellor, who, according to Marsalek, was managing his “secret campaign financing.”

Marsalek then shared a link to an article about the corruption allegations against Kurz and the phone which had been seized from one of the leader’s closest associates, Thomas Schmid, a former senior official in Austria’s Finance Ministry.

Schmid’s phone had been seized in November 2019. The extensive communications recovered from the device subsequently became important evidence in several corruption investigations.

In October 2021, prosecutors carried out raids involving Kurz’s government and his political party, the ÖVP, over allegations concerning the misuse of public money for politically favorable opinion polls and media coverage. 

Pressure from the investigation led to Kurz announcing that he was stepping down. Two weeks later, Marsalek wrote to Roussev that it was “quite a messy story”.

Later in the conversation, he referred again to the political consequences of the information recovered from the phone, saying: “And the rest of the chats ‘killed’ the chancellor.”

The documents contain no independent evidence that Marsalek actually organized the seizure of the phone.

Russian ties

Marsalek’s links to Austria’s former domestic intelligence service, the BVT, have been investigated extensively and a number of senior spies and police officers are accused of handing him information for use by the Russian state.

The messages between Marsalek and Roussev are contained in Austrian police files investigating “support for a foreign intelligence service – interference in Austrian politics.” The documents also refer to possible offenses relating to elections, breaches of official duties and corruption.

An assessment of the messages by investigators notes that “Marsalek stated unequivocally that ‘they’ had ‘toppled’ the chancellor in a successful operation.”

“Marsalek thus admitted to Roussev that he had been involved in the confiscation of this mobile phone,” the report continues

The investigators therefore interpreted the conversation as Marsalek claiming involvement in the seizure of a phone that had contributed to the chancellor’s downfall.

The same assessment notes that it remained unclear whether Marsalek’s reference to “the guy” who had worked “for us” meant Wirecard or a Russian intelligence service.

Kurz declined to comment on the messages or the investigators’ assessment.

At the time the messages were sent, Marsalek was living in Moscow and carrying out work primarily for Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), British prosecutors have said.  

Roussev was one of a number of Bulgarians arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying on behalf of Russia. They were later convicted and Roussev was jailed for ten years and eight months.

The group organized surveillance operations targeting Kremlin opponents and investigative journalists and discussed kidnapping as well as planning disinformation campaigns.

The network also had access to sensitive Austrian government information. In May 2025, The Telegraph revealed that three mobile phones belonging to senior Austrian Interior Ministry officials had ended up in Russia.

These were different phones from Thomas Schmid’s device, which Austrian investigators seized in November 2019. No connection between the two incidents has been established.

Kurz’s downfall

The reference to a confiscated phone concerns one of the most important pieces of evidence in Austrian political corruption investigations of recent years.

Schmid was a senior figure in the Finance Ministry and a close associate of Sebastian Kurz. He later became head of the state-owned holding company ÖBAG.

His mobile phone was seized by Austrian investigators on November 12, 2019, and police recovered extensive communications, including messages that had previously been deleted.

Those messages later became part of several corruption investigations concerning political appointments, government advertising and allegations about the use of public money for party-political purposes.

On October 6, 2021, Austrian prosecutors searched the Federal Chancellery, the Finance Ministry and the headquarters of Kurz’s Austrian People’s Party.

The searches were part of an investigation into allegations that taxpayer money had been used to finance politically favorable opinion polls and media coverage.

The investigations led to Kurz announcing his resignation as chancellor on October 9, 2021.

Marsalek’s message to Roussev was written 13 days later, nearly two years after Schmid’s telephone was seized.

By then, details of the case including reports about thousands of intimate photographs on Schmid’s phone, which Marsalek joked about, had already appeared in the local press.

Marsalek has been out of reach of European authorities for years, and the Global Reporters Network was also unable to contact him for comment.

“The Russian secret services like causing havoc and chaos and disruption,” Ed Arnold, senior associate fellow at Royal United Services Institute think tank, told the Global Reporters Network. “But even if they don’t cause it, they are more than happy to exploit it and make political disagreements or fissures worse.”

He said Marsalek might have been “overplaying his hand” by emphasizing his role in the downfall of Kurz, adding: “If you want to make a name for yourself in this world as some kind of fixer, you need some kudos.” 

“Russia wants to destabilize our free democracies,” Manfred Weber, the German leader of the EPP in the European Parliament, told POLITICO. “It must be unequivocally ruled out that Russian intelligence services can interfere in democratic and judicial processes … These events must be thoroughly investigated.”

A spokesperson for the Federal Ministry of the Interior said that they could not comment on ongoing investigations into Marsalek’s network. 

The spokesperson told the Global Reporters Network that the “Austrian Criminal Intelligence Service does not provide information or comment on ongoing investigations or proceedings, nor does it disclose information concerning specific individuals”.

]]> de Merz’s conservatives poised to nominate Germany’s first woman president https://www.politico.eu/article/merz-conservatives-poised-nominate-ilse-aigner-first-woman-president-germany/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 06 Nov 2026 20:02:13 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9288681 BERLIN — Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner is set to become Germany’s next president, making her the country’s first woman to hold the office, according to two senior conservatives with knowledge of the matter.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) will nominate Aigner to succeed outgoing German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the officials told BILD, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. Both officials were granted anonymity to discuss internal party matters freely. Aigner’s nomination will officially be announced Monday, according to the officials.

Aigner, who previously served as agriculture minister under former German Chancellor Angela Merkel from 2008 to 2013, is currently president of the Bavarian State Parliament. The CDU and CSU form a joint parliamentary bloc in the Bundestag and are part of the European People’s Party in the European Parliament. Merz intends to inform senior CDU politicians Sunday that Aigner will be the bloc’s candidate, the two officials said.

Steinmeier’s second five-year term ends in March 2027. He is not eligible for re-election. His successor will be elected on Jan. 30, 2027. The German presidency is largely ceremonial, with the chancellor setting the government’s policy agenda.

Bavaria’s CSU premier, Markus Söder, suggested Aigner as a candidate back in April. The CSU has long dominated Bavarian politics but has never produced a German chancellor or president. Prominent SPD and Green politicians have also signaled their support for Aigner in recent weeks.

Brandenburg’s SPD state premier, Dietmar Woidke, described Aigner as “the perfect candidate” who knows German politics “inside out,” he told POLITICO’s Berlin Playbook on Friday.

]]> en Trump’s ‘big, beautiful’ European security plan isn’t convincing Europe https://www.politico.eu/article/jared-kushner-european-security-plan-is-not-convincing-europe/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 06 Nov 2026 17:58:32 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9287796 BRUSSELS — Europe is once again watching the White House through gritted teeth.

An opaque Trump administration proposal for a new European-wide security arrangement with Russia has met skepticism from European capitals that fear it risks sidelining the continent and emboldening Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin.

“We already have a European security architecture in place — NATO and European Union both have their respective roles,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Friday in reaction to the U.S. plan. “We must make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture. The latest U.S. proposal underscores growing anxiety around Trump’s fresh rapprochement with Russia as he ramps up pressure on Ukraine and his administration attempts to revive long-stalled talks to end Moscow’s full-scale war against Kyiv.

POLITICO spoke to 12 NATO diplomats, EU envoys and European government officials, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue. NATO allies were not briefed about the American plans in advance, according to three alliance diplomats, and many remain skeptical of the idea.

“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner added soon after.

Kushner said the arrangement would have five goals: “Permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” 

“It is a bit obscure what Kushner meant,” said one NATO diplomat. “The general sentiment in Europe is that any discussion with Russia on the future architecture at the moment will just be used by Moscow to legitimize their arguments … it will not fly with the European allies.”

A senior European official added: “Literally, there’s nothing to find fault with, but we know there’s something else going on.”

‘The elephant in the room’

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s top adviser, Björn Seibert, briefed EU ambassadors on Friday, according to two EU diplomats, following a discussion between national security advisers on the issue.

“There’s willingness to engage in Kyiv and in the rest of Europe although there’s little confidence in the Russians — but the EU is not blocking it,” one of the EU diplomats said after the meeting. But “the group around Trump underestimated how important the conflict is for Europe and how a bad outcome for Ukraine is very dangerous for Europe.”

“It’s a long-standing position for us and many others that European security architecture should not be discussed while there is a war,” said a senior European security official. “And obviously not without Europeans.”

“Europe must have a seat at the table in negotiations on peace in Ukraine and the future European security architecture,” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda added Friday, after a meeting of the eight Nordic and Baltic countries.

This week saw two rounds of working-level meetings in Brussels on a Ukraine peace deal, ahead of U.S.-brokered working-level talks with Ukraine and Russia on Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.

“We must be realistic about the peace talks and we must be very careful when it comes to the real intentions of Russia,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a group of reporters, including from POLITICO, earlier this week. “In winter, Putin might have less incentives to get a deal.”

Stefan Kornelius, spokesperson for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — who talked to Trump on Thursday night — said: “A new sense of urgency has … emerged” on negotiations after this week’s U.S. midterm elections, adding the issue would resurface at an informal gathering of EU leaders in Dublin next week.

The meeting had been intended to focus on AI, but developments in Ukraine could overshadow the talks, a third EU diplomat said. “Things are moving pretty fast,” they said.

Still, some allies fear the U.S. may tie its new initiative to an upcoming review of American troops in Europe, expected in December. 

“That’s the elephant in the room,” said a second NATO diplomat. “One thing is talking about European security architecture … with an ‘ordinary’ U.S. posture; another thing is to talk about a European security architecture ‘as things will be,’ and nobody knows how that’ll be.”

]]> en NATO faces €7B shortfall on military aid pledge to Ukraine  https://www.politico.eu/article/nato-faces-7b-euro-shortfall-military-aid-pledge-ukraine/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 06 Nov 2026 17:20:31 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9280143 BRUSSELS — NATO allies face a €7 billion funding gap for Ukraine this year as Russia steps up its bombing campaign and Kyiv calls for more air defenses.

NATO’s 32 member countries agreed in July to provide €70 billion in military aid to Ukraine in 2026 and an equivalent sum in 2027.

But the alliance now faces a shortfall of around €7 billion, with less than two months until the end of the year, according to three alliance diplomats, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely. It is unclear where exactly the current gap is coming from, but it is likely to hamper Ukraine’s ability to buy vital equipment to fend off Russian missiles and drones this winter.

The shortfall comes ahead of an alliance meeting on Nov. 17 where European capitals are expected to examine ways to boost funding and increase the transfer of critical weapons to Ukraine. While new NATO funding pledges are still expected, it’s possible that allies may fail to meet this year’s target, the diplomats said.

A NATO official speaking on behalf of the organization said that “allies continue to provide essential military support to Ukraine” to fulfill the pledge and “are working to ensure that Ukraine has the support it needs now and into the future.”

The target combines bilateral contributions throughout the year and €30 billion drawn from the EU’s €90 billion loan to Ukraine.

Kyiv has repeatedly urged allies to step up their funding as Russia continues its devastating air assaults; more than 40 people were reportedly killed after a school bombing this week.

During a closed-door meeting with allies Thursday, Ukraine’s ambassador to NATO Alyona Getmanchuk “emphasised the importance for Ukraine of NATO Allies fulfilling the commitment made at the Ankara Summit to provide €70 billion in military support this year,” according to a statement by the Ukrainian mission.

“It is essential to mobilise all partners to the fullest extent, accelerate new decisions, and translate previously announced commitments into concrete deliveries of equipment or transfers of funds,” it added.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has also asked allies to dig deep for more money. “With winter coming, and with Russia’s aggression unrelenting, allies need to do more, especially in support of air defense,” he said during a recent visit to Tallinn.

The missing cash underscores the growing difficulties faced by allied governments in continuing to finance Ukraine. The U.S., once the main giver, has stopped almost all new aid since Donald Trump returned to the White House.

That has left European countries as Ukraine’s key supporters. But many capitals face growing fiscal strains while countries such as Germany, the Netherlands and Nordic nations — which have historically provided outsized contributions — have repeatedly called on others to give more.

There is “some fatigue” from the largest donors “[which] have repeatedly financed packages,” the third NATO diplomat said.

NATO’s Ukraine funding is typically channeled toward programs like the alliance’s non-lethal aid scheme, called the Comprehensive Assistance Package, as well as its Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List that has European allies buying critical U.S. weapons like Patriot interceptors for Kyiv. The shortfall includes a $1.9 billion gap in funding for unpaid PURL deliveries, two of the diplomats said.

Separately, allies remain skeptical that they will meet Rutte’s target of $15 billion for PURL this year. “I do not think that there’s a chance we will meet that,” said the same NATO diplomat cited above.

Ukraine’s NATO mission said 29 allies have now contributed to the scheme. Since its launch in 2025, it has raised around $9 billion in total contributions, the two diplomats added.

]]> en Wave of bomb threats target Irish media outlets and more European flights https://www.politico.eu/article/bomb-threats-target-irish-media-and-more-european-flights/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:50:31 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9287778 DUBLIN — Bomb threats targeting several of Ireland’s top media organizations are almost certainly linked to next week’s European Political Community summit in Dublin, a government official told POLITICO.

Newsrooms at Irish national broadcaster RTÉ, Virgin Media TV, the Irish Independent newspaper and Newstalk radio received identically worded emails Friday morning claiming bombs had been left inside their offices.

Three of the newsrooms were evacuated, disrupting RTÉ and Newstalk programs, while Virgin staff kept broadcasts running. Police confirmed they found no suspicious devices.

“We have expected a rise in hybrid threats to Ireland because of our hosting of the EU presidency, and the EPC meeting will be by far the biggest set-piece event of that presidency, so one must presume it’s no coincidence that we’re experiencing this spike in hybrid activity now,” the Irish official said.

The Irish government said the threats against media outlets were probably part of a European-wide pattern of threats that have targeted dozens of airlines this week, including Irish carriers Ryanair and Aer Lingus. Hackers also targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

“It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralized or coordinated effort,” the Irish government said in a statement. “However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.”

Bomb threats also targeted at least 18 European flights Friday, after at least 22 the day before, raising concerns that the hoaxes may be part of a coordinated campaign to disrupt air traffic.

Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares told Spanish public broadcaster TVE on Friday that the bomb threats affecting flights could be “an attempt at hybrid aggression and war in some psychological way.” He added that “it cannot be a coincidence that so many identical events occur with the same modus operandi throughout Europe.”

Luis Gallego, CEO of airline group IAG, said: “It is clear that what they [the perpetrators] are looking for is to create chaos and disruption in the different airports.”

Fighter jets were scrambled in Hungary on Friday “in response to bomb threats involving three civilian passenger aircraft,” said Hungary’s Defense Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi.

Prague Airport said nine flights were targeted by bomb threats Friday alone, while France reported another four threats against aircraft flying over its territory that day. The Bulgarian government told AFP that two flights bound for Sofia were targeted by bomb threats on Friday.

Aviation professionals have said no threat should be underestimated. “No matter how remote the real possibility after a call that there is a bomb on board, we will treat it as if there is a bomb on board,” said Paul Reuter, an airline captain and vice president of the European Cockpit Association.

The Irish government official told POLITICO that the sudden increase in anonymous disruptions to airlines, supermarkets and now news outlets appeared to be timed to increase tensions ahead of Dublin’s hosting next Thursday of the EPC summit.

Created in 2022 following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EPC brings together the leaders of 47 European countries and representatives of several bodies, including NATO, to discuss strategic issues. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is also attending.

The Irish official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss Friday’s threats freely, declined to identify Russia as the likely culprit. But he noted that EU partners — including Denmark, which faced a similar wave of so-called hybrid attacks in the run-up to its own 2025 hosting of the EPC — had drawn such links in the past.

Irish police Superintendent Liam Geraghty said the event posed an even tougher security challenge than hosting a U.S. presidential visit. “We have not seen a policing and security operation of this scale ever before in Ireland,” Geraghty told reporters.

The leaders, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, write that the agreement is “necessary to unlock the full potential of the North Sea” and to “transform it into the largest clean energy hub in the world.”

“An agreement will thus enhance Europe’s energy security and contribute to a competitive economy that centres on access to clean and affordable energy,” the letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa states.

“These benefits underline the importance of swiftly concluding the ongoing negotiations. We call on you and the UK to agree during the Summit on a path towards the conclusion of these negotiations.”

Britain’s energy industry says the agreement could help bring down electricity prices in the U.K. — a cost-of-living priority for Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Energy UK, the industry’s representative body, says that being outside the electricity market will create “additional costs of up to £10bn this Parliament through higher energy bills and lower Treasury revenues.”

The same EU diplomat quoted above, from a country supportive of a swift agreement, said the financial contribution required to rejoin the market would amount to “investing” in market access.

“A larger electricity market will ultimately lead to lower electricity prices in the U.K. And of course, the U.K. is currently facing very high electricity prices,” they said.

“The U.K. would be investing in access to a more integrated, secure and competitive European energy market — bringing lower energy costs, greater investment certainty and huge opportunities for British businesses and consumers.”

Greater security of supply, more price stability, and greater certainty for investors would also be key benefits, they said.

While talks on the internal electricity market are not expected to conclude in time for this month’s summit, the Nov. 20 meeting is expected to see both sides sign off three further agreements on youth mobility, emissions trading and alignment on agri-food rules.

Brussels and London are also expected to issue a “joint statement” at the meeting which will address other issues, including the future of talks on the internal electricity market.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Sun, 08 Nov 2026 19:53:59 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Heart-breaking Kraków attack can make Poland stronger https://euobserver.com/247697/heart-breaking-krakow-attack-can-make-poland-stronger/ Sun, 08 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247697 Rightly or wrongly, many of my Polish friends immediately feared that the Kraków killer had been groomed by Russia. "The rate of these incidents is growing exponentially and it's hard to think they're not connected," said one contact.]]> I heard the news about Kraków from my daughter, with whom I visited the Market Square some 10 years ago, so it felt very personal.

On top of my shock, it didn’t make sense: Why would a far-right terrorist murder their own people?

So the simplest explanation seemed to be that he was a psychopath acting on individual motives.

But it came after police arrested a knifeman at the Polish Constitutional Tribunal protests on 31 October.

It also came after three stabbing attacks in Polish schools over four days earlier in October.

And Polish police foiled a far-right terrorist plot to bomb a mosque in September.

So my bigger worry is that Kraków was a symptom of a wider social sickness, caused by radical online content and political hate speech in Poland, which meant there could be more of these ‘lone wolf’ attacks in future.

“This is bound to happen sooner or later if radical sentiments are constantly being fuelled in society,” a Ukrainian friend and former intelligence officer told me, referring to extremism on social media and in the rhetoric of Polish rightwing and far-right parties, the PiS, KKP, and KWiN.

But many of my Polish friends immediately feared the worst scenario – that the Kraków killer, or the other attackers on my list, had been groomed by Russia, as part of its by now well-documented campaign of terrorism and hybrid warfare against Europe, which is designed to break Western support for Ukraine.

“The rate of these incidents is growing exponentially and it’s hard to think they’re not connected,” said one Polish friend and official.

“I don’t have any evidence, but I’ve got a strong gut instinct on this one [Kraków]. Trust me, Andrew, it’s an element of Russian warfare, it’s designed to cause panic, and we’re going to see more of it,” he added.

A second Polish friend said: “We live in crazy times. I suspect ‘someone’ [Russia] put him [the Kraków gunman] up to this.”

And if you think that sounds like our typical Russophobia, then a former Russian intelligence officer I know had the same gut feeling.

“This is just the beginning. There will be more such incidents,” he told me on Sunday (8 November).

We can’t a priori attribute every train crash, riot, or political murder in Europe to Russia, even if it does exploit them all to harm us.

]]> Europe’s democratic renewal is coming from the margins — and Brussels still isn’t listening https://euobserver.com/247287/europes-democratic-renewal-is-coming-from-the-margins-and-brussels-still-isnt-listening/ Sun, 08 Nov 2026 10:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247287 None of Serbia, Albania or Bosnia and Herzegovina are full EU members. Brussels generally approaches them as recipients of European democratic standards, not as teachers. But what if Europe's democratic renewal comes not from its political centres, but from its edges?]]> On 25 October, Serbia’s student-led movement won a parliamentary majority, defeating an entrenched establishment after nearly two years of protests.

What began as outrage over a deadly railway station collapse in Novi Sad became a nationwide challenge to corruption and the exercise of power.

In Albania, the “Flamingo Protests” are challenging a luxury tourism project threatening protected wetlands.

Read more

Kushner‑backed luxury project in Albania becomes a litmus test for EU accession green standards

Women in Bosnia and Herzegovina who defended their river from hydropower development have taken their solidarity across the border to support Albanian communities fighting for theirs.

None of these countries are full European Union members. Brussels generally approaches them as recipients of European democratic standards, not as teachers.

But what if Europe’s democratic renewal comes not from its political centres, but from its edges?

Europe faces two connected democratic failures. The first is a failure to listen. The second is a failure of belonging. Looking to Europe’s edges could help address both.

The peripheries

First, Brussels has long treated the continent’s peripheries as resources to be used or problems to be managed. Ports move goods. Borderlands police migration. Coastal regions supply energy and tourism. Candidate countries receive instruction on democratic standards. Even when the centre consults local populations, it generally arrives with the questions already written and the solutions largely decided.

The political traffic generally runs in one direction: ideas flow outward from Brussels, while labour, energy and strategic assets flow inward. Rarely does Europe ask what its margins know that its centres do not.

Yet borderlands, divided cities, islands and ports confront Europe’s most pressing questions firsthand.

Who belongs? Who decides what development means? How do people share land, water or public space when their histories and loyalties collide? How does a community act together without agreeing on everything? These are not abstract policy puzzles. They are questions of daily life, answered through negotiation, cooperation, conflict and compromise.

Read more

Serbia’s Student List has been inspirational, but the big test will be forming a stable anti-corruption government

Serbia’s student movement challenged entrenched power through collective mobilisation. Albania’s protesters are asking who gets to decide whether a coastline is a public good or a private opportunity. And Bosnian river defenders have shown that political solidarity can cross a border rather than end at it.

None offers a blueprint for Europe. All offer practices worth learning from.

Europe’s second failure runs deeper. Liberal democracy rightly defends rights, constitutional safeguards and equal citizenship. But constitutional patriotism— the hope that shared loyalty to democratic rules can bind diverse societies— has too often proved too thin to satisfy people’s hunger for belonging.

Institutions can protect freedoms without giving citizens a sense of common purpose. A legal framework is essential. It is not, by itself, a political community.

Learning from the margins

Populists have seized this opening. Ethno-nationalist movements offer something that procedural liberalism often struggles to provide: attachment, solidarity, heritage and a story about who “we” are. But they build that belonging by excluding others. Their answer to a genuine democratic need is to make political community narrower and more fearful.

Europe cannot answer this threat simply by repeating its commitment to liberal norms. Nor should it concede the desire for rooted, meaningful belonging to those who would turn it into a weapon.

Here, too, the margins have something to teach. In places where neighbours inherit incompatible memories, where livelihoods depend on contested resources, and where borders cut through relationships, people sometimes build common purpose without first becoming alike. Shared work, obligations, arguments and care for a place can produce attachments stronger than abstract agreement and more generous than ethnic sameness.

We should not romanticise these practices of course.

Local solidarities can be exclusionary; informal compromises can entrench injustice. And winning an election is not the same as governing democratically. But refusing to idealise the edges is not a reason to ignore them. It is a reason to examine their political experiments with the seriousness routinely granted to ideas born in European capitals.

The two failures are connected. When Brussels sees the edges only as territories to administer, it overlooks the democratic practices through which people develop belonging. And when liberal politics neglects belonging, it leaves the field open to the far-right.

The answer is not another programme dispatched from the centre.

It is a reversal of the direction of learning. Let communities help define the questions before policy is written. Treat their experiments in shared life, public resources and contested heritage as sources of political insight, not colourful local anecdotes. Bring their ideas into Europe’s democratic debate.

Serbia’s victory does not prove that the margins have all the answers. It makes an uncomfortable possibility harder to dismiss: Europe may be searching for democratic renewal in the very places it has been taught to overlook.

]]> ‘A photograph allows us to really stare’: new Brussels exhibition documents modern human slavery, ahead of EU Parliament debate https://euobserver.com/247592/a-photograph-allows-us-to-really-stare-new-brussels-exhibition-documents-modern-human-slavery-ahead-of-eu-parliament-debate/ Sat, 07 Nov 2026 09:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247592 A Brussels photography exhibition on modern slavery opened this week, exposing the cruelty of contemporary human-trafficking, often against women and girls, ahead of MEP discussions on the EU's new strategy.]]> A new photography exhibition examining modern slavery opened this week in Brussels – ahead of European Parliament discussions on fresh strategies against such human trafficking.

In the Nepalese mountains, a woman comes back to her village with jewellry and shining trinkets, giving the appearance of wealth. She promises local kids jobs in Kathmandu.

“The whole village supports the kids going…. What they didn’t know is she was trafficked,” Lisa Kristine, an American photographer profiling human trafficking victims, told EUobserver.

The “Slavery: Stories of the Present” exhibition opened on Thursday (5 November) in Géopolis, a city-supported photo-journalism museum in Brussels.

It features works of two photographers focusing on modern slavery around the world and on women and girls in rural Afghanistan, often forced to marry in their early teens.

About 50 million people were enslaved as of 2022, with some 27 million in forced labour, and 22 million married against their will, according to the International Labour Organisation data. The number grew by 10 million since 2016.

Many are sold off to pay for family debts, others are lured with false promises of good job conditions. 

Read more

‘Younger and younger victims’: EU faces challenge of AI-fuelled online sex trafficking

In the EU alone, at least 880,000 people are forced to work, including 270,000 being sex-trafficked.

Photography, argues Kristine, one of the two photographers whose works make up the exhibition, is a good method of raising awareness on the topic: contrary to statistics or even an eye-to-eye encounter, “a photograph allows for us to really stare.” This way, the viewer can take the time to see the other person and open up to empathy.

“The issue is rather abstract, full of data… but when you actually see a human being, it speaks more to your heart,” Kristine told EUobserver.

Pictures by the other photographer, Élise Blanchard, show Afghan girls and women, whose families have often lost their herding grounds or could no longer farm on their land as a result of climate change. Selling their daughters for marriage is a way out of family debts.

“I’m not trying to frighten somebody or overwhelm somebody with something horrific…” she said, highlighting the human dignity she tries to show through her portraits.

]]> Italy still obstructing asylum returns from other EU states amid simmering dispute that threatens Schengen https://euobserver.com/247568/italy-still-obstructing-asylum-returns-from-other-eu-states-amid-simmering-dispute-that-threatens-schengen/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:21:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247568 Italy's foot-dragging on taking back asylum seekers from other EU states is contributing to a simmering dispute that risks shattering whatever trust has been restored among member states on the Schengen border-free travel zone.]]> Rome is still not fully accepting the return of prospective asylum seekers from countries such as Germany even though they first entered Europe on Italian territory, in a simmering dispute that could potentially erupt and place further pressure on the EU’s border-free travel zone.

A document released on Friday (6 November) by the European Commission says transfer requests were still being rejected as of the end of September.

“Based on the information provided by the member states between 12 June and 30 September 2026, transfers requested by other member states continued to be rejected by the Italian authorities,” says the document.

“Furthermore, according to information received, there have been cases in which the Italian authorities returned persons to the transferring member states, despite Italy having been determined as the member state responsible,” it added.

Even though it says Italy, as of 29 October, has resumed transfers, according to an administrative letter, the European Commission couldn’t determine if anyone had actually departed for Italy.

The findings highlight a politically-explosive scenario whereby arriving asylum seekers fan out through the rest of Europe, triggering knee-jerk reactions by member states to impose internal border controls on the Schengen area.

It also echoes the scenario whereby Italy slapped border controls on Spain over the summer over unfounded fears that the tens of thousands of people that entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta would somehow end up on continental Europe.

Italy has for years allowed people to leave without first registering them, in a process of self-relocation that has angered other EU states. Many travel through France to reach northern Europe.

The internal EU discussion will take place at an informal summit in Dublin on 13 November, following an exchange of letters between EU Council president António Costa and Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who bewailed the current “disarray” of various European diplomatic formats on the war.

The Dublin meeting will focus on the “profile, format, and mandate” of the job, leaving till later proposals on individual names, an EU source said.

Meloni told Costa that “I am not asking for this role for myself or for Italy”, but did not rule herself out either.

]]> EU prosecutors launch possible €110m fraud probe into Spain’s railways, after second lethal crash https://euobserver.com/247457/eu-prosecutors-launch-possible-e110m-fraud-probe-into-spains-railways-after-second-lethal-crash/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:06:21 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247457 Spain is under investigation for its spending of €110m in EU development funds granted for planned renovation of the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line, following a second deadly accident on the high-speed line in 2026.]]> The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) on Friday (6 November) launched an investigation into the Spanish state railway for possible fraud of EU funds for maintenance of the line that saw a second deadly collision this year on 28 October.

The EU’s independent prosecutor in Madrid launched the probe into the use of European funds following the crash on the Madrid-Seville high-speed rail line that killed 69 people in Toledo last week, while an earlier accident in January left a further 46 dead on the same route. 

The EPPO’s headquarters in Luxembourg announced they launched investigative measures into Spain’s Administrator of Railway Infrastructure (ADIF), its State Railway Safety Agency (AESF) and the Court of Auditors in Spain. 

The European Commission stayed silent on the procedures when asked at a press briefing on Friday, since EPPO procedures are launched independently of EU institutions.

Read more

Two fatal train disasters in less than a year: I never thought I would see this happen in my native Spain

Agents of the Civil Guard visited both offices on Friday morning, to request documents that may show any evidence of embezzlement of European funds in the maintenance works of the high-speed rail line.

]]> Russians repel attack by Ukrainian ground-robots armed with RPGs, in futuristic assault (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,716) https://euobserver.com/247493/russians-repel-attack-by-ukrainian-ground-robots-armed-with-rpgs-in-futuristic-assault-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1716/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:29:51 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247493 Ukrainian commander Andriy Biletsky is gambling on mass robot assaults to spare his soldiers’ lives, as Russian troops rush to prove on camera that they can still swat the machines from the sky and fields around Lyman. ]]>
  • Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps is saving lives by sending robots into attacks.
  • In Orikhiv and Mala Tokmachka, Russians are being pushed out of built-up areas.
  • Even after more than half a year, Z-patriots cannot fully admit defeat in Dnipropetrovsk region, but fear the situation in Komar.
  • The death toll from the attack on Komyshuvakha has risen to 53.
  • Kyiv has been plunged into darkness, without water or sewage services — Russia is attacking more intensely, and the capital was unprepared.
  • The effectiveness of shooting down drones is improving very slowly.
  • Maps of the day — Orikhiv. Velyka Novosilka direction.
  • Videos of the day — what the failed ground-drone attack looked like from the Russian perspective; Kyiv without electricity; a MiG-29 shot down a drone with its cannon at point-blank range; a Geran-5 crashed into a field; a new type of interceptor drone.

    • Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps sent dozens of robots into an attack. This was the same formation that carried out the successful Vivaldi operation near Lyman.

    During that operation, the corps had already used various innovative methods of deploying drones. Among other things, heavy aircraft transported armed ground drones deep behind Russian lines, catching Russian defences by surprise.

    Now, units under the command of Andriy Biletsky tried another innovation. So far, the course and outcome of the fighting are known only from Russian sources. Other information may emerge over time, but for now the attempt can be considered unsuccessful.

    Nevertheless, it is an extraordinary example of how an army suffering from a manpower shortage and seeking to protect its limited resources uses modern technology. It also suggests how drones could help break the deadlock at the front and shift from static to mobile warfare.

    The Russians claim that as many as 28 drones attacked without the direct involvement of a single Ukrainian soldier in combat.

    The Russian Telegram channel Military Informant counted two drones armed with US-made Mk 19 grenade launchers, 18 drones equipped with two RPGs each, and eight kamikaze drones loaded with explosives among those involved in the attack.

    ]]>         EU states back one-year methane delay, but leave door open for more https://euobserver.com/247446/eu-states-back-one-year-methane-delay-but-leave-door-open-for-more/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:23:32 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247446 Member states agreed a one-year delay to the EU’s methane rules, with a built-in option to delay again next year.]]> EU ambassadors on Friday (6 November) agreed to delay the EU’s methane rules for oil and gas imports by one year, but added a review that could push them back further.

    At the third attempt in a matter of weeks, member states backed the Irish council presidency’s compromise, which keeps the commission’s proposed one-year delay timeline. 

    Read more

    Importers would have to start monitoring, reporting and verifying the methane emissions of the oil and gas they buy abroad from 1 January 2028 instead of January 2027.

    Reporting on the methane intensity of imported oil, gas and coal would be postponed to 5 August 2029, and maximum intensity limits would apply from 5 August 2031, one year later than planned.

    But the compromise also asks the EU Commission to assess whether importers are actually able to comply with the rules, before 30 September next year.

    ]]>         From India to Africa, renewables race ahead but Europe is lagging, IEA report shows https://euobserver.com/247441/from-india-to-africa-renewables-race-ahead-but-europe-is-lagging-iea-report-shows/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:05:51 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247441 The Iran war has pushed governments from India to sub-Saharan Africa to build more solar and wind, with some regions almost tripling new capacity. But in Europe, that rollout is stalling. ]]> The oil and gas shock from the Strait of Hormuz is speeding up the transition to renewables almost everywhere in the world, but not in Europe, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its annual renewables report on Friday (6 November).

    The Paris-based agency expects global renewable power capacity to grow by almost 4,800 GW between 2026 and 2031, which is 57 percent more than in the previous six years. 

    But it cut its expected growth forecast for Europe by six percent compared to estimates made last year, although Europe will still add around 100 gigawatts (GW) a year until 2031.

    Migrating is an obstacle course that takes a toll not only on bodies but also on mental health. Léa stresses that every phase of migration is traumatic: before crossing the border, during the crossing, and also on arrival. Migrants are experiencing wars, sometimes death and distress.

    As a result, they are more likely to develop post-traumatic stress, depression and anxiety. On top of this, there is the case of people who already had mental health problems beforehand and can no longer be followed up or treated correctly. 

    So how do authorities take that into account? Let’s be clear: access to psychosocial care is very limited in the support provided to migrants.

    A presidential veto override needs two-thirds of both chambers, and in the Senate most ordinary bills still need 60 votes to get past a filibuster. Democrats have neither. They will control spending bills and they can subpoena officials. 

    They can also block or delay nominees, which is enough to slow the administration down but not enough to run foreign policy from Capitol Hill.

    Congress already authorised $400m [€356m] a year for Ukraine security assistance in 2026 and 2027, in the defence law it passed last December.

    Democrats can push actual money through must-pass spending bills. A president cannot lawfully refuse to spend appropriated funds for policy reasons. 

    Presidential drawdowns from US stocks, delivery schedules and export licences remain largely in executive hands.

    Trump lost his emergency tariffs in the Supreme Court in February. He replaced them with a temporary global levy. When that expired on 24 July, new tariffs on imports from 60 economies took effect the same day, under a different law.

    Congress could rewrite the powers it delegated to the president, but that bill would meet a veto. Even Joe Biden, a president friendly to Europe, needed months to ease the steel tariffs after Trump’s first term, and he replaced them with quotas, not free trade.

    On Iran, war powers resolutions face the same veto, and attaching conditions to war money is politically hard while American troops are in the field. Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz carried oil and petroleum products equal to about a fifth of world consumption.

    Most of it went to Asia, but major disruptions still push up the prices Europeans pay.

    On Nato membership itself, the protection is stronger. A 2023 provision co-written by Marco Rubio, then a Republican senator from Florida and now Trump’s secretary of state, bars withdrawal from Nato without two-thirds of the Senate or an act of Congress.

    Whether it holds against a president who claims treaty withdrawal as his own power has never been tested in court.

    Congress went further a year ago. The December 2025 defence law limits what Pentagon money can be used for in Europe. It cannot pay for cutting US forces there below 76,000 for more than 45 days.     The restriction applies to fiscal 2026 funds, and Congress is considering whether to extend it.

    Even if it survives, the law covers what is stationed in Europe. What Washington sends when a crisis comes, and whether aircraft based in Germany fly for European purposes or for operations somewhere else, is still decided in the White House and the Pentagon.

    The timing is bad too.

    The Pentagon’s review of US forces in Europe was to give secretary of defense Pete Hegseth at least four sets of options by 6 November, with the review finished in December.

    The new Congress only meets on 3 January, so Hegseth is scheduled to have the options weeks before any Democrat chairs a committee.

    A YouGov poll of more than 7,000 people across France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Romania and Spain found that support for unlimited pesticide approval stands at between four to six percent in France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland and Spain, and 10 percent in Romania. The poll was commissioned by Pan Europe, an environmental lobby group.

    Meanwhile, hefty majorities of between 68 percent (in Spain) and 80 percent in Romania say that pesticides should be phased out completely. The survey also found that opposition to increased pesticide use prevails across the political spectrum, with conservative and centre-right voters only marginally more in favour of deregulation on pesticides than greens and leftists. 

    However, the survey findings are at odds with the direction of the “Food and Feed Safety” proposal tabled by the EU Commission last December and, in particular, of leading MEPs who want to deregulate more than the commission. 

    The commission proposal would make unlimited approvals for pesticide active substances the norm, scrapping the regular safety reviews that have allowed 54 harmful substances to be banned since the EU pesticide regulation entered into force in 2011. 

    Under the existing rules, pesticides are approved for a limited period and must be reassessed every 10 to 15 years. 

    “The message is clear: unlimited pesticide approvals have no public support, not even from conservative and far-right voters. MEPs pushing to weaken pesticide safeguards are out of step with the people they represent”, said Salomé Roynel, policy officer at PAN Europe.

    ]]>         Details emerge of Russian atrocity: dropping three-tonne bombs on civilians at food bank and shelter (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,715) https://euobserver.com/247163/details-emerge-of-russian-atrocity-dropping-three-tonne-bombs-on-civilians-at-food-bank-and-shelter-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1715/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 14:21:55 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247163 Newly released police body-camera footage and analysis by independent Russian investigators puncture Moscow’s claims they hit a “military target”, exposing how rescue workers and civilians were lured into a shelter in Komyshuvakha before being annihilated. ]]>
  • Harrowing footage from a police body camera shows that Russians were attacking civilians in Komyshuvakha.
  • Monday’s attack is the deadliest in terms of casualties since at least 2023.
  • What Russian propaganda says about the war crime — and why independent Russian analysts also dismiss it as lies.
  • October figures on frontline shifts according to Finland’s Black Bird Group: Russians barely moved.
  • Charts of the day: Russia lost more aircraft than tanks in October.
  • Videos of the day: FPV drones hang from wires like birds; the difficult journey of Russian logistics.

    • The largest attack on civilians in at least the past two years. World media have focused on the US elections in recent days, and so it has somewhat gone unnoticed that Russia committed one of the largest attacks on civilians in Ukraine since the start of the war.

    It happened on Monday morning in the village of Komyshuvakha in Zaporizhzhia oblast, around 15 km from the front line.

    Source: DeepState UA

    On Monday morning, Russians attacked the school complex, where humanitarian aid was being distributed to local residents.

    In total, they dropped at least nine glide bombs, some of them weighing three tonnes. Such a bomb weighs roughly twice as much as a Škoda Octavia car and contains up to 1.4 tonnes of explosives. Russia primarily uses these bombs to destroy underground bunkers.

    This time, however, they did not hit Ukrainian soldiers but civilians.

    What happened: By Thursday morning, it was known that at least 42 people had been killed in the attack on Komyshuvakha. This alone makes it the worst attack on civilians in Ukraine since 2023.

    A further 33 people remained missing, apparently buried beneath the rubble. It is therefore quite possible that the total death toll will rise significantly, making this the worst attack on civilians since the bombing of the theatre bearing the word “Children” in Mariupol in 2022.

    It is one of the worst things Russia has done during the war. Russian propaganda, however, has sought to portray the attack differently. It claims that the site of the attack was a base for Ukrainian soldiers or police officers.

    On Wednesday, Ukrainians released harrowing footage recorded by a camera attached to a police officer’s body. It suggests that the Russians knew full well whom they were attacking.

      <title>Trump may have lost but don’t bet Democrats can fix the economy</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/07/democrats-economy-affordability-crisis</link>
      <description><p>There’s not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over prices</p><p>It was the economy, again. Although Donald Trump largely ignored it, voters’ acute concerns over the rising cost of living fuelled a political upheaval for the ages that is likely to deliver the biggest swing toward Democrats since Watergate, granting them the largest House majority in nearly four decades alongside their biggest edge in the Senate since 2008.</p><p>Still, having come to power promising to restore affordability, the new crop of Democrats are soon to discover that there is not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over pricey gas and groceries, exorbitant mortgages and unaffordable healthcare.</p><p>Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter <a href="https://eduardoelreportero.substack.com/">Being There</a> on Substack</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/07/democrats-economy-affordability-crisis">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/06/us-job-growth-october</link>
      <description><p>‘Low-hire, low-fire’ labor market shows sluggish growth but few layoffs, with an interest rate hike expected in December</p><p>The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid ongoing war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.</p><p>Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/usemployment">unemployment rate</a> went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/06/us-job-growth-october">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Rural voters were feeling left behind before the midterms, poll shows</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/former-trump-voters-economy</link>
      <description><p>Polling done for the Guardian shows plummeting support from a former key constituency of Donald Trump’s base</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/nov/05/what-happens-after-the-blue-wave-our-reporters-answer-your-midterm-election-results-questions">Q&amp;A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>Polling conducted by the Harris Poll for the Guardian before the election shows just how angry voters were and points to one key reason Republicans lost so badly: plummeting support from rural voters, once a key constituency of Donald Trump’s base.</p><p>Over the summer, 95% of Americans indicated they believed there was an <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/jul/07/cost-of-living-poll-groceries-gas">affordability crisis</a>, particularly because of steep gas and grocery prices. By October, 61% of voters <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/voters-economy-cost-of-living-prices-poll">believed</a> the country was experiencing a recession, even though technically it wasn’t.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/former-trump-voters-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US stocks rise, dollar slides as investors digest Democrats’ midterm victories</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears</link>
      <description><p>Government bond yields fall while initial fears ease over impact of election results on world’s biggest economy</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/04/midterm-elections-results-senate-house-michigan-maine-mississippi-latest-updates">US midterm elections – live updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/explainer-midterms-trump-us-global-economy-markets">After US midterms, what will lame-duck Trump mean for global economy?</a></p></li></ul><p>US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a>, lifted by hopes that <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy.</p><p>The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, its best day in over a year, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&amp;P 500 gained about 1.5% each when markets closed on Wednesday afternoon, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/03/midterm-election-results-live-updates">won control</a> of the Senate and the House of Representatives.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Fox News pundits hardly criticized the US president in midterms coverage but Trump was still quick to cast blame</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/05/midterm-elections-live-latest-updates-mississippi-senate-race">US midterms 2026 live – latest updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/nov/03/midterm-elections-full-results-senate-house-governor-races">Track live results from all 50 states</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/nov/05/what-happens-after-the-blue-wave-our-reporters-answer-your-midterm-election-results-questions">Q&amp;A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>In the weeks leading up to Tuesday’s midterm elections, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/28/trump-fox-news-truth-social">Donald Trump made clear that he would place some blame on his favorite cable channel</a>, Fox News, if his party did poorly.</p><p>On election day, he didn’t disappoint.</p><p>This article was amended on 4 November 2026; a previous version incorrectly stated that Karoline Leavitt is Donald Trump’s most recent press secretary, when it is in fact Katie Zacharia.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/trump-blames-fox-news-republican-losses">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>CVS Health to split pharmacy chain from health insurance</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/cvs-health-pharmacy-insurance</link>
      <description><p>CVS Pharmacy will be separate from CVS Health, housing major insurer Aetna and benefits manager Caremark</p><p>CVS Health, the largest US healthcare conglomerate valued at $117bn, has announced its plans split off its pharmacy chain from its <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/healthinsurance">health insurance</a> and benefits businesses, ending an era in which healthcare companies grew into vast conglomerates.</p><p>In their announcement on Wednesday, CVS Health said they will split off its 9,000 pharmacies, in-store clinics and mail order prescription business into a business named CVS Pharmacy.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/cvs-health-pharmacy-insurance">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Semi-retired professor Carolyn Marvin became a local celebrity facing down Philadelphia’s growing robot delivery army: ‘It’s my first amendment right to protest’</p><p>“One of you needs to be on the lookout for cops, while I block the robot, OK?”</p><p>It is a crisp fall morning in Philadelphia. <![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comMon, 09 Nov 2026 02:22:07 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[How do I work out Revenue taxation of my retirement ARF when its value changes all the time?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/08/how-do-i-work-out-revenue-taxation-of-my-retirement-arf-when-its-value-changes-all-the-time/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/08/how-do-i-work-out-revenue-taxation-of-my-retirement-arf-when-its-value-changes-all-the-time/Sun, 08 Nov 2026 10:30:42 +0000I retired last year at the age of 60 and started drawing an income this year from my ARF (Approved Retirement Fund). I believe that at the age of 61 Revenue requires that I withdraw a minimum of 4 per cent. I have seen in some places that November 30th is the date to calculate the minimum imputed distribution. (It is not clear if this is the value on November 30th in the current year or the preceding year.)

I would like to understand this calculation as I am taking a fixed value in income each month, but the total value of the fund fluctuates daily. So I would like to understand how I can ensure that for the total tax year I meet the 4 per cent minimum requirement.

PK

ARFs are an increasingly popular option for people looking at options for the pension fund they have built up over a working life. They allow people to keep their fund invested even after retirement.

In bygone days when most pensions were defined benefit schemes, this wasn’t important. Your employer guaranteed to pay you a set sum in retirement based on your years of service and your final salary.

Big shortfalls in occupational pension funds against expected liabilities meant employers moved rapidly away from such guarantees, which became promises to pay “where possible”. Inevitably, over a fairly short time, employers sought to shift pension risk further from themselves to their employees and we moved to a defined contribution model, where a worker’s retirement income is determined by the amount invested by the employee and the employer and the investment performance of those sums.

Defined benefit schemes do remain in the public service and in a rapidly diminishing number of private sector companies. But these days, for most people, all the risk on retirement income rests with the worker, none with the employer.

When they retire, those workers are entitled to draw down a tax-free lump sum and then to invest some or all of the pension fund balance either in an ARF or in an annuity – an insurance product that guarantees to pay a certain sum each year for the rest of your life.

Biggest difference to your pension pot is not how much money you put in

You can inflation-proof annuities and provide for a pension for a spouse who might survive you, but these products have, for many years, been poor value. That’s why ARFs have become increasingly popular.

As you say, there are rules around how you will be taxed on your ARF, imposed by Revenue after a small number of people tried to game the system in a manner it considered to be calculated tax avoidance.

Imputed distribution

If your pension fund is worth more than €2 million, Revenue will tax you on the basis that you have withdrawn 6 per cent of your fund each year. That’s not an issue for most people as very few funds will be anywhere close to €2 million.

For the rest of us, you will be taxed on the presumption that you have drawn down 4 per cent of your fund each year while in your 60s, rising to 5 per cent once you turn 70.

This is called “imputed distribution”. In your case, Revenue is essentially saying that even if other sources of income mean you only need to draw down, say, 2 per cent of your fund, it will apply tax on the basis of a 4 per cent drawdown.

In that scenario, clearly it makes sense to draw down and get the use of that 4 per cent. Who wants to pay income tax and USC on money they have not even enjoyed the use of?

And that brings us to this November date. To assess what this 4 per cent (or 5 per cent depending on age) looks like, Revenue requires a fund valuation on November 30th each year. That sets the mark against which tax will be assessed.

Managing your money and your time in retirement

On instinct, it makes sense that you would be looking at November 30th the previous year, not least because November of the current year is late in the tax year to have to adjust your spending.

However, Stephen Rice, propositions lead at Aviva Life & Pensions Ireland, assures me this is not the case.

“The relevant valuation date is November 30th in the current tax year,” he tells me.

“Assuming the ARF holder was aged 60 or over for the whole of 2026, was not aged 70 or over for the whole year, and their combined ARF and other relevant retirement funds did not exceed €2 million, the applicable amount [of imputed drawdown] would be 4 per cent of the fund value at November 30th, 2026.”

Given we are now in November, this means the valuation date is looming.

Rice gives the example of a pension fund valued at the end of this month as being worth €100,000. Revenue will assume that at least €4,000 has been drawn down this year by the ARF holder.

How big should your pension pot be for a comfortable retirement in Ireland?

If you had left the ARF untouched all year, that means you would need to draw down €4,000 in December to match the “imputed distribution” figure. But, like most people, you have been drawing down a fixed sum each month this year from this fund so you will likely be close to this figure anyhow.

Fund values can change daily, as you point out. To take just one very basic measure, as of the end of last week, the broad-based S&P 500 index in the US was up 7.5 per cent so far this year. A couple of days earlier, the year-to-date gain was 12 per cent.

The November 30th valuation date allows you adjust your drawdown in December to ensure that you meet the imputed distribution figure.

If, by year end, you have drawn down more than 4 per cent of the fund, you will be taxed on what you have drawn down rather than the 4 per cent figure.

For most retirees, the trickiest feature of the ARF is that it makes them responsible alongside their fund manager and any adviser for ensuring that the fund delivers sufficient income to provide reasonable income in retirement.

As the €176 billion in Irish deposits indicates, the vast majority of Irish people choose to have nothing to do with personal investment, so suddenly making such decisions in retirement – or even having the basic financial literacy to consider them – is a challenge in a world where all the risk rests with the individual.

Don’t make an additional voluntary contribution to your pension – until you read this

On a straight-line basis and assuming no change in fund value, an ARF should last 21 years before being exhausted for someone who retires at 66 and draws down the minimum required.

However, investment is never that simple. Returns fluctuate up and down, leaving you with the risk that you could find your fund has been exhausted before you die.

And, regardless of investment performance, there is always the impact of fund charges to consider. You would be surprised at how these can impact your fund over time.

The whole point of an ARF is that your funds can continue to grow in retirement through investment gains – rather than being set against a moment in time with an annuity – but that does require the ARF holder to keep an eye on the performance of their fund and, if necessary, consult their fund manager or adviser about making changes if required.

Having said that, volumes of investment history confirm that regular chopping and changing of investment strategy is rarely to your advantage. Always remember that investment is a longer-term game, even in an ARF where the risk level for the vast majority of us will be relatively low.

In funding retirement, hopefully your fund is more substantial than the €100,000 used in Aviva’s example, but the figures still show what imputed distribution means for you this year and in the years ahead.

Please send your queries to Dominic Coyle, Q&A, The Irish Times, 24-28 Tara Street, Dublin 2, or by email to dominic.coyle@irishtimes.com with a contact phone number. This column is a reader service and is not intended to replace professional advice.

]]><![CDATA[Singapore overtakes Ireland as Apple’s biggest tax shelter]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/08/singapore-overtakes-ireland-as-apples-biggest-tax-shelter/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/08/singapore-overtakes-ireland-as-apples-biggest-tax-shelter/Sun, 08 Nov 2026 15:48:48 +0000Apple shaved $2.7 billion (€2.4 billion) off its tax bill this year by channelling earnings into Singapore, according to new disclosures that reveal how the city-state has become the tech giant’s biggest tax shelter.

The figures, filed together with Apple’s annual report under new US reporting requirements, reveal the company took advantage of Singapore’s tax incentives regime to lower its bill after attributing as much as $50 billion in profits through its Asian hub in 2026.

Its savings in Singapore exceeded the $2.6 billion reduction it achieved via Ireland, Apple’s European headquarters, the disclosures published this week show.

“While Apple’s reliance on Ireland was first revealed more than a decade ago, the enormous tax savings in Singapore are a major revelation,” said Zorka Milin, codirector of the Fact Coalition, a Washington-based tax transparency group.

Apple declined to comment.

The savings show that even after more than a decade of concerted global effort to level the playing field on corporate taxation, large US tech groups continue to reap the rewards of accumulating profits in low-tax jurisdictions.

The filings are part of new US federal accounting rules that require US-listed companies to divulge when their tax on overseas profits differs significantly from the statutory federal rate, which is 21 per cent.

If Apple had been taxed on all of its global profits in 2026 at the US federal rate, it would have incurred a total bill of $33 billion – demonstrating the scale of the $5 billion tax reduction it received from booking profits in Ireland and Singapore. The company incurred corporation taxes totalling $27 billion this year.

Many US multinationals do not pay the 21 per cent federal rate on all their US income because of domestic deductions and tax credits. However, the differential between this rate and the tax incurred elsewhere indicates which overseas jurisdictions a company derives the greatest tax benefit from.

Apple has faced intense scrutiny over its use of offshore hubs to reduce its tax bill. The tech giant was forced to repay more than €13 billion in Irish taxes with interest after a high-profile 2016 EU state aid investigation found it had illegally benefited from tax breaks in the country.

Sales between subsidiaries can allow multinational companies to move profits out of high-tax jurisdictions and into low-tax ones, a strategy known as profit shifting.

The backlash against such manoeuvres led to a landmark deal in 2021, in which countries led by the OECD agreed to introduce a minimum effective corporate tax rate of 15 per cent.

Many low-tax jurisdictions, including Ireland and Singapore, aligned themselves with the OECD effort, with some anticipating an exodus of multinational companies as they raised their tax rates.

But this flight has so far not materialised, allowing the countries to collect windfall tax payments.

Singapore, for example, clawed back $2.5 billion from Apple in 2026 via a top-up tax it implemented last year as it aligned with the OECD initiative.

Mike Lewis, director of investigative think tank TaxWatch, said the global minimum tax set a relatively low floor, meaning that “to some degree, it’s business as usual for some of these companies”.

Others have argued that companies’ decisions to remain for now in these jurisdictions are a sign they are there for reasons aside from low taxes, such as skilled workforces, infrastructure and stable political and legal frameworks.

Apple’s biggest Singaporean subsidiary is a sales and marketing hub, selling products and services to Apple entities overseas and “developing intellectual property”, its accounts show.

Across its two main Singaporean entities, Apple generated about $9 million in pretax profit per employee in 2024, the latest year for which figures can be calculated.

In Ireland last year, Apple’s pretax profit per employee was $6 million. Across the world in 2025, the equivalent figure was less than $1 million.

These vast disparities show the mismatch between the size of Apple’s workforce in these jurisdictions and the substantial profits accrued there.

Singapore rolled out the OECD rules for financial years starting in 2025. Its headline corporate tax rate is 17 per cent, exceeding the global minimum tax, but companies can negotiate incentives that reduce this rate.

The US disclosures indicate Apple benefits from such arrangements, which offer relief and credits for activities deemed by Singapore to be of high economic value.

From 2023 to 2025, Apple’s effective tax rate in Singapore fluctuated about 10 per cent, accounts for its main local entities show.

This year and in the future, the top-up taxes levied as part of the OECD initiative are likely to take the rate closer to 15 per cent.

In 2025 Apple booked pretax profits of nearly $40 billion in its Singaporean subsidiaries, according to their latest published accounts.

This year, the figure could be as high as $50 billion, Financial Times estimates based on the US disclosures suggest.

“We’re starting to get an idea of just how much lost [tax] revenue is being left on the table, billions of dollars just for this one company in a single year,” said Milin, of the Fact Coalition.
