]]><![CDATA[The magnificent one: Apple is winning by sitting out the AI spending race]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/08/the-magnificent-one-apple-is-winning-by-sitting-out-the-ai-spending-race/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/08/the-magnificent-one-apple-is-winning-by-sitting-out-the-ai-spending-race/Sun, 08 Nov 2026 06:18:00 +0000Forget the magnificent seven. Apple has become the magnificent one.

Up over 25 per cent in 2026, the iPhone maker is back on top of the stock market, with a valuation of $5 trillion putting it ahead of Nvidia.

Creative Planning strategist Charlie Bilello recently noted Apple was the only magnificent seven stock to outperform the S&P 500 this year.

The contrast with 2025 is striking. “AI is turning Apple into a market ‘loser’”, headlined Axios in July 2025, a message echoed by Bloomberg (“Apple faces calls to reboot AI strategy with shares slumping”).

Criticised for spending too little on AI, Apple now benefits as investors fret about how much its rivals are spending. Apple generates more free cash flow than any other magnificent seven member, while avoiding the AI spending binge “draining” its peers, says Bilello.

Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta spent a combined $202 billion on capital expenditure in the third quarter alone, more than double the year-earlier figure. Concerns over Alphabet’s cash burn sent its shares down 19 per cent in October, their worst-ever monthly performance.

Apple, which reported earnings on Monday, has essentially become a hedge against the AI trade, outperforming the Nasdaq-100 by almost 20 percentage points over the past six months.

Given its recent run, with shares up 25 per cent since June and $1 trillion added to its market value, Apple has arguably done well simply to hold on to those gains amid the recent market turbulence.

Ironically, the flight to safety has not come cheap. Apple trades at 36 times expected earnings, almost twice the S&P 500 multiple. Apple’s AI issues remain, but its reluctance to spend heavily is looking less foolish as the bills mount up elsewhere.

Brown<![CDATA[Effects of Unite case being quietly felt in courts two years on]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/08/effects-of-unite-case-being-quietly-felt-in-courts-two-years-on/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/08/effects-of-unite-case-being-quietly-felt-in-courts-two-years-on/Sun, 08 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000It’s not only the unions that talk about the waves made by the Supreme Court’s decision in Unite’s case against HA O’Neill a couple of years back. Legal experts are talking about them too.

Last week, at an Irish Congress of Trade Unions event, former chair of the Labour Court Kevin Duffy argued that Chief Justice Donal O’Donnell’s observation in his judgment on the case that “the right to form unions would be of little benefit if the activities of the union and its members were to be regarded as presumptively unlawful” might have the effect of undermining the Government’s claim that it cannot legislate to require employers to engage in collective bargaining in certain circumstances due to constitutional issues.

It is, Duffy suggested, simply a question of political will.

On Friday, Cathy Maguire SC pointed to another of the judgments in the case, that of Judge Brian Murray, as having hinted at the possibility of a right to strike being recognised at some point in the future.

“It is arguably implicit in Article 40.6.1 iii of the Constitution that the right to form trade unions implies in turn at least some – perhaps as yet undefined – zone of freedom for those unions to organise and campaign,” he wrote.

The observation, Maguire made clear, did not do anything to actually recognise such a right but, she said, Murray “raised the question” that it (the constitutional right of freedom of association) “may in the future be held to encompass a right to strike”.

The more immediate benefit to unions already appears to be evidenced in the absence, since the court delivered its decision two years ago, of cases taken by employers seeking injunctions intended to thwart strike action.

]]><![CDATA[Ireland’s towns offer part of the solution to the housing crisis. We should seize it now]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/07/irelands-towns-offer-part-of-the-solution-to-the-housing-crisis-we-should-seize-it-now/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/07/irelands-towns-offer-part-of-the-solution-to-the-housing-crisis-we-should-seize-it-now/Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Mass dereliction and vacancy blights almost all Irish market towns. You’ve seen it for yourself: once bustling commercial centres are lifeless, hollowed out by dilapidation and urban neglect. As shopping places, most towns are barely hanging on and the more we insist that ground floors be reserved for retail space, the more widespread the sense of abandonment will become. The future of shops is not the main street, but that doesn’t mean the main street has no future, it just has one that looks different.

Shopping in the 21st century is not like shopping in the 20th or 19th centuries when most of our market towns were built. According to Eurostat, 96 per cent of Irish internet users made online purchases in 2024, the highest share in the European Union. We are rejecting the idea of the local town as a retail destination but people still want to live, socialise and hang out in towns. Is there a way to achieve this and the attendant footfall, without forcing all ground floors to be shops? What about abandoning the notion that shops should be at street level?

This week, the State nudged its way towards this by announcing a new plan that will encourage businesses to move into vacant shopfronts in towns. Rolled out across 26 designated town centres, the initiative will target empty retail properties. Rather than shops, the new plan envisages that businesses or services might move in instead. Welcome as this is, it is not enough and probably has more to do with the fact that business rates pay a chunk of county council revenue, which councils want more than innovative new town planning.

A small town in Co Kerry and a formula for rejuvenating rural Ireland

Most towns in Europe were originally derived from medieval constructs, built around commercial fairs where farmers bought and sold their produce. Around such markets, basic urban life, with artisans, money lenders, churches and taverns eventually developed. Commerce was geographically centred – the town was the locus of commerce. Urban evolution was determined by commerce. As agricultural productivity grew and fewer workers were required on the land, the urban population expanded. If you were an artisan and lived in an urban environment, your existence and life experience were quite distinct from that of your ancestors, farm labourers on the land who were beholden to some hereditary knight or feudal baron. In the town you were more free, leading to the German expression “stadtluft macht frei” (“urban air makes you free”). Floating in the air of the city were radical ideas of individual sovereignty, encouraging for the dissenter or outsider. The word ‘bourgeois’ comes from these newly commercial people who lived in the ‘burgh’ or the town.

Of course, the economic history of towns and small cities predates medieval times. For example, the Greek empire was made up of many dozens of free, self-governing city states. To organise this new type of society, a new idea emerged: the polis. By the sixth century BC, the polis – or the town – was firmly established as the foundation of all Greek civilisation. Obviously the word politics derives from it. The polis was the civic, social, economic, military and political cornerstone of ancient Greece and the rules of the polis outlined citizens’ rights and obligations. The Greek polis was organised around the agora, the marketplace, a space not just for the exchange of goods but for ideas and sedition too.

This is a crisis. Maybe it is time to phase out the requirement that properties in urban centres must be commercial, whether business or retail

Today, commerce and the market for ideas has moved from our towns to our phones, from the street to online. These trends are not absolute, but they are sufficient to have changed the way we rest, work and play. Possibly the biggest change has been the inability of local or provincial retailing to compete with out-of-town supermarkets, big city retail and, of course, online shopping, not to mention working from home, which naturally takes people away from commercial centres. Last year, 990,600 Irish people worked from home, nearly 30 per cent of the total workforce. Urban commerce is feeling the pinch. GeoDirectory data shows the retail and wholesale sector in Ireland lost 434 occupied commercial units, a bigger fall than any other sector. Meanwhile, retail insolvencies continue to rise, jumping 35 per cent in the first six months of this year.

David McWilliams: Ireland will not have any political peace until we fix housing

Urban planning struggles to catch up. For example, despite the fact that retail commerce is leaving our towns, one of the State’s main answers to urban neglect, the Department of Housing’s €95,000-€135,000 vacant-above-the-shop grant still clings to the notion that people are shopping in town. The grant applies only where “the ground-floor commercial use continues”. The pressure that empties shopfronts is met by a grant that requires them to stay open. If the shop can’t survive there is no grant to do up the property, and the property therefore remains empty. The effect of this grant means the fortune of urban repopulation is tethered to shops, which are a symptom of the problem rather than the solution. Meanwhile, the housing shortage is in its second decade and our vacant towns – with their existing connection to utilities and the heritage of the buildings – remain idle.

Reviving small Irish towns: ‘They are exactly the same as some of the finest European towns. They can become vibrant communities again’

According to the GeoDirectory commercial report there are 30,611 vacant commercial units in Irish towns. The national number conceals a disparity. The highest vacancy rates are to be found in towns in Donegal (20.7 per cent), Sligo (20.2 per cent) and Galway (18.6 per cent), while the lowest rates of urban vacancy are in Meath (9.9 per cent), Wexford (11.2 per cent) and Westmeath (12 per cent). Meanwhile, the most boarded-up town in Ireland is Shannon in Co Clare with 34.9 per cent vacancy. Of all commercial properties vacant, Carrigaline, Co Cork, had the lowest at 5.1 per cent. Above the shop, things are worse: the Heritage Council cites upper-floor vacancy of about 80 per cent in historic town centres. Meanwhile, ground-floor retail vacancy is about 20 per cent in many towns – well above the European average of 5 per cent.

This is a crisis. Maybe it is time to phase out the requirement that properties in urban centres must be commercial, whether business or retail. Dutch towns, for example, have deliberately shrunk their shopping areas, concentrating shops in a compact core and converting the fringe streets to homes: 9,000–10,000 homes are being created from vacant shops.

As Ireland’s market towns wither away, it is time to realise that we are facing massive global shifts in the way we live, and these shifts demand immediate remedial action, rather than incremental small measures. Our towns offer part of the solution to the housing crisis. We should seize it now.

]]>PAUL FAITH<![CDATA[Are we ready for the AI bubble bursting?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/07/are-we-ready-for-the-ai-bubble-bursting/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/07/are-we-ready-for-the-ai-bubble-bursting/Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Artificial intelligence (AI) has many – mostly far from fully understood – implications for humanity. Among these is something concrete and current: it has launched a huge surge in spending on physical capital, to meet the demand for huge data centres.

Indeed, according to a fascinating paper, Financing the AI Buildout by Stijn van Nieuwerburgh of the Columbia Business School, spending in the US will average 3.6 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) from 2025 to 2032 (inclusive).

This would be larger than the average of 2.2 per cent of GDP spent on railways between 1870 and 1890, let alone the 1.1 per cent spent on highways from 1956 to 1973. In fact, it would be the biggest sector-specific investment boom of all.

Some of those earlier transformations were sustained over far longer periods. But this fact makes the AI buildout even more concentrated and so, quite possibly, even more disruptive.

Moreover, as van Nieuwerburgh explains, financing the boom is now creating some classic risks, despite the strength of the huge companies (mainly Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle) driving the huge surge in spending.

Moreover, these risks are also macroeconomic. Booms can easily turn into busts, as stock market valuations collapse, companies go bankrupt, lenders lose money and planned investment vanishes. Will this time be different? Ultimately, that depends on the profitability of the new businesses and, in this case, hopes are very high indeed.

A small Irish business was hit by a cyberattack linked to infected online ad. Then came the ransom demand

As the paper points out, aggregate capital expenditures by the companies listed above rose from $97 billion (€87 billion) in 2020 to $416 billion in 2025 and a forecast of $801 billion in 2026. In 2020 the surplus of operating cash flow of these companies over capital spending was $155 billion.

In 2025 they still had a cash-flow surplus of more than $187 billion. But over these years, the ratio of capital spending to operating cash flows rose from 38 per cent in 2020 to nearly 69 per cent in 2025.

Then, in 2026, according to the companies’ forecasts, capital spending will exceed cash flow by $93 billion and the ratio of spending to cash flow will hit 113 per cent.

Alphabet and Microsoft will still spend a little less than their cash flow. But Oracle’s spending will be 138 per cent above it, Amazon’s 36 per cent above it and Meta’s close to it.

As a result, ever more complex financial arrangements are being made. Thus, not for the first time, an investment boom is causing an explosion in leverage. While the hyperscalers’ direct investment is still important, “the marginal financing model is shifting. Specialised data centre developers, REITs, infrastructure funds and private equity investors increasingly build or acquire facilities and lease capacity to hyperscalers and other large users.”

The result, according to the paper, is an increasingly complex and nontransparent financial structure. In particular, it notes, “publicly rated debt represents only a relatively small share of the data center financing; much larger volumes are provided through syndicated bank loans and private-credit facilities, for which little information is publicly available.”

Former Musk aide urges Ireland to modify its approach to data centres

In sum, “the central issue is not simply that AI infrastructure is exposed to technological and operating risks, but that the sector’s financing structure can transmit and amplify those risks.”

This is historically familiar behaviour. Risks for data-centre owners include: concentration in the tenants and also in sources of final demand; technological obsolescence and so the need to scrap and replace relatively quickly; and political and operational difficulties involved in making the investments work.

Moreover, van Nieuwerburgh adds, “Chip designers, cloud providers, data centre operators and infrastructure investors increasingly depend on one another through long-term contracts, strategic investments and financing arrangements.” This creates fragility.

These are not just issues for the AI sector itself. The investment boom is big enough to have large macroeconomic implications. A paper from the Federal Reserve suggested that spending on computer hardware, software and data centres contributed more than a percentage point to annualised quarter-over-quarter US GDP growth in the first quarter of this year, partially offset by a half a percentage point of GDP increase in net imports in those categories.

Both the IMF’s World Economic Outlook and a recent Substack from Matt Klein shed light on the international spillovers of the global AI boom, especially on to Taiwanese and South Korean products.

A crucial question, however, is how far the AI mania has infected the stock market, above all in the US. Here some of the vulnerabilities are evident. First, the Magnificent Seven (Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla) have, until recently, been pulling the US stock market ever higher.

Second, the market is at valuations rarely seen before, with a cyclically adjusted real earnings yield of 2.5 per cent, which is only fractionally above the current real interest rate. This makes sense only if earnings from stocks are about to grow far faster than ever before.

In the past, however, whenever earnings have been this low relative to stock prices, the latter have crashed. Is this AI-driven boom, with all its unavoidable uncertainties about future profitability, returns on the huge and rapidly growing investment, and now the elaborate financial engineering, going to be any different?

The longer the investment boom and the associated financial engineering continue, the bigger the negative economic impact is likely to be when it ends.

This does not mean that AI itself will fail to be the transformative technology it seems to be, though only a species that adores playing Russian roulette would tolerate a business (Anthropic) whose prospectus says it could create “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.

New technologies have often triggered stock market manias and investment booms that end in busts. Recent market tremors suggest this could even be happening to AI now. A return to reality will come when it will come. The readiness is all. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Ritchie B Tongo<![CDATA[Can a focus on simplicity give Google’s Fitbit the Edge? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/review/2026/11/07/can-a-focus-on-simplicity-give-googles-fitbit-the-edge/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/review/2026/11/07/can-a-focus-on-simplicity-give-googles-fitbit-the-edge/Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000To screen or not to screen? A lightweight tracker that bridges the gap between screenless and full smartwatch.

]]><![CDATA[Planners approve Gas Networks Ireland’s €200m investment to cut emissions]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/planners-approve-gas-networks-irelands-200m-investment-to-cut-emissions/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/planners-approve-gas-networks-irelands-200m-investment-to-cut-emissions/Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Planners have given Gas Networks Ireland (GNI) the go ahead for a €200 million plan to slash carbon emissions, the State company has confirmed.

GNI operates the network that supplies natural gas to homes and businesses in Ireland from domestic and international sources.

Planners in Dumfries & Galloway Council in Scotland have given the Irish company permission for €200 million worth of work on key parts of a pipeline that supplies 80 per cent of this country’s gas.

GNI intend to fit electric motor drives to compressor stations on the Moffat Interconnector, which connects Ireland’s system to a broader European network from which it imports large quantities of natural gas.

According to the company, the project will cut its overall carbon dioxide emissions by 87,000 tonnes a year, a 42 per cent reduction, while maintaining the pipeline’s reliability.

Ireland imports gas through the interconnector, mostly from Britain or Norway, so the compressor stations are key to the country’s energy security.

The stations compress the gas to maintain the pressure needed to transport it through undersea pipes that connect with Ireland’s own network.

The electric motors will replace existing turbines driven by natural gas, cutting emissions to zero.

GNI says the project is part of a wider plan to cut greenhouse gas emissions from its operations.

Dumfries & Galloway Council’s ruling covers compressor stations at Beattock and Brighouse Bay in southwest Scotland.

Natural gas is used to generate around half this country’s electricity needs, while it provides energy to manufacturing, particularly the pharmaceutical industry, responsible for much of the Republic’s lucrative corporate tax returns. Many homes use the fuel for heating and cooking.

GNI’s director of assets and infrastructure, Brian Sheehan, welcomed the council’s decision.

“Around 80 per cent of the gas we use in Ireland passes through these stations,” he noted.

Sheehan added that they played a key role in the country’s energy security.

“The planning permission is a positive step forward in delivering this infrastructure and we continue to work closely with stakeholders in Ireland and Scotland as the project progresses,” he said.

]]><![CDATA[NTA pays firm more than €110,000 per month since 2023 for communications advice]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/nta-pays-firm-more-than-110000-per-month-since-2023-for-communications-advice/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/nta-pays-firm-more-than-110000-per-month-since-2023-for-communications-advice/Sat, 07 Nov 2026 05:25:00 +0000The business of building public transport infrastructure is an eye-wateringly expensive one, as Irish taxpayers know only too well.

The latest projected price tag for the MetroLink rail project in Dublin is between €14.4 billion and €17.5 billion, having soared over the past four years. Hands up who thinks it will be delivered within that range?

Then there’s BusConnects projects for Dublin and Cork, Dart+ and a raft of other projects.

This might help to explain the large sums being paid for external public relations and communications advice by the National Transport Authority (NTA).

In response to a recent question from Social Democrats TD Aidan Farrelly, Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien said that following a tender process in 2022, the NTA awarded the communications contract to Dublin-based Q4PR. The communications firm is led by its founders Angie Kinane, Gerry O’Sullivan, Martin Mackin and Jackie Gallagher.

“The combined team comprises 13 personnel supporting the delivery of the BusConnects Dublin programme, BusConnects Cork and regional cities and active travel projects, as well as engagement activities for other major sustainable transport programmes, including Dart+ and MetroLink,” the minister’s reply stated.

That’s a lot of people working externally to assist in shaping the messaging around these transport projects, and helping to manage relationships with various stakeholders.

And the cost of this advice?

Some €1.2 million was paid to Q4 in both 2023 and 2024, rising to just over €1.5 million in 2025 and €1.5 million so far in 2026. It adds up to a total of more than €5.4 million over the four years.

On average, that’s north of €110,000 per month for the firm or €415,000 per Q4 staff member over the period.

It’s worth noting, too, that the NTA has its own in-house media team, led by head of communications Jennifer Gilna, while MetroLink has its own director of communications, Eoin Murphy.

Quality and results drive Q4PR’s growth, according to its website. Lucrative contracts from State agencies clearly help, too.

Polish prosecutors have announced the opening of a terrorism investigation following Saturday’s attack in the city of Kraków, where a man opened fire from his vehicle, killing six people. Later, three further bodies – believed to be the perpetrator’s parents and sister – were found in his home.

Further details have also emerged regarding the victims of the attack, the heroic actions of police and medical personnel, as well as the attacker himself – though the motive for his actions remains unknown.

On Saturday, the suspected attacker, who has been named only as 24-year-old Michał O. under Polish privacy law, drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, including its famous market square, which was packed with tourists and locals.

He fired at random from the car, killing six people. Three of those victims have been identified as Polish women, aged 47, 53 and 61. Another was a 32-year-old British man. The final two victims were a foreign woman aged 51, whose nationality has not yet been announced, and a Polish man in his 50s.

A further 16 people were injured in the attack, 11 of them Polish. The interior ministry has said that, among the dead and injured are citizens of the UK, Austria, Germany, Russia and Portugal.

Two of the injured are police officers who pursued the attacker and engaged in a firefight with him. They and Michał O. were hospitalised with what have been described as critical injuries. Due to his ongoing medical treatment, law enforcement authorities have not yet been able to formally take the suspect into detention.

CCTV footage shows the moment two police officers confront the Krakow shooter. pic.twitter.com/vcQ0Xvi1nX

— WarMonitor🇺🇦🇬🇧 (@WarMonitor3) November 7, 2026

However, on Sunday morning, the National Prosecutor’s Office announced that it has launched a formal investigation into the killing of six people in Krkaów and the attempted murder of numerous others. The actions are being treated as a terrorist offence.

Meanwhile, they are also investigating the killing by gunshot of three people in the town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, also on Saturday. That is Michał O.’s hometown, and on Saturday evening Prime Minister Donald Tusk revealed that three bodies had been found at the address where he lived.

Prosecutors say that “the evidence indicates that the same person committed the acts” in both Kraków and Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski.

Previously, on Saturday evening, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński announced that initial findings indicate the suspect had “very radical far-right views”. However, he cautioned that investigators were still seeking to confirm this, as well as to understand the possible motive behind the attack.

Minister @MKierwinski na konferencji w Krakowie: 💬 Sprawca mógł być zafascynowany ideologiami skrajnie prawicowymi. Ten wątek będzie jednak szczegółowo weryfikowany. Czynności prowadzą funkcjonariusze @PolskaPolicja, jak i @ABW_GOV_PL – na miejscu zdarzenia oraz w domu rodzinnym… pic.twitter.com/PppmMPmWYW

— MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) November 7, 2026

Gun crime is exceedingly rare in Poland, which has one of the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe. Saturday was the first time that the country has experienced a mass public shooting of this type.

In response, a period of two days of official public mourning has been declared, with a decree to that effect signed by President Karol Nawrocki and Tusk.

Meanwhile, political leaders have praised the heroic actions of police, especially the two officers, Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański, who were critically injured while bringing Michał O’s rampage to an end.

“They are heroes,” said Krzysztof Klęczar, governor of the Małopolska province in which Kraków is located. “Considering how many weapons were still in the perpetrator’s car, if it weren’t for the effective and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher.”

 

It has also emerged that the police officers were treated by two leading surgeons who, by complete chance, had been eating dinner with their families at a restaurant near where the final shootout took place.

One of them, Michał Pędziwiatr, a professor of surgery at the Jagiellonian University, told the media that he and fellow surgeon Mateusz Wierdak had seen the police subduing the attacker. While their families took shelter, the two doctors rushed to the scene once the shooting had finished.

“Mateusz’s dedication in stopping the bleeding of the most injured police officer [Kulik] undoubtedly saved his life,” Pędziwiatr told the Fakt newspaper. Pędziwiatr himself called a local hospital that he knew would be best equipped to treat the officer so that they could prepare for his arrival.

⚫️"Tato, strzelają do ludzi!". Lekarz ujawnia kulisy zamachu

Prof. Michał Pędziwiatr i dr Mateusz Wierdak byli w pobliskiej restauracji, gdy doszło do strzelaniny. Zanim przyjechały karetki, lekarze udzielili pomocy rannym. – Wyszliśmy na zewnątrz. Już się żegnaliśmy. Nagle mój…

— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) November 8, 2026

Public authorities in Poland, including the police and military, launched a drive for blood donations to help in the treatment of Kulik, who remains in critical condition. They said they had been overwhelmed by the number of people coming forward.

The defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, also revealed that Kulik is a former soldier from the elite 6th Airborne Brigade, which is headquartered in Kraków. “The entire military community is proud of Jakub. We will support him and his loved ones,” wrote Kosiniak-Kamysz.

A public fundraiser launched by Krzysztof Stanowski, a prominent media personality, has, at the time of writing, raised over 3.5 million zloty (€777,000) to support the police officers and their families.

On Sunday morning, Klęczar also confirmed that Michał O. had “undergone several surgeries during the night” and “remained in critical condition”.

❗Kiedyś żołnierz 6 Brygady Powietrznodesantowej, dziś policjant i bohater- starszy posterunkowy Jakub Kulik, który wczoraj został ranny w zamachu w Krakowie potrzebuje naszego wsparcia.

Ranny policjant przebywa w szpitalu. Potrzebna jest krew grupy AB Rh+.

Krew można oddać…

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 8, 2026

The authorities have confirmed that Michał O. holds a firearms licence. During the incident on Saturday, he appears to have used an AR-15-style rifle, but police also found a number of other firearms in his vehicle.

On Sunday morning, a shooting club in the town of Starachowice that media reports suggested had been used by Michał O. and his father issued a statement saying that the suspect “has never been trained in dynamic, tactical or combat shooting in our club”.

They added that the club is fully cooperating with the authorities to provide any necessary and relevant information for the investigation.

]]> Six killed in terrorist shooting in Polish city of Kraków https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/07/fatalities-reported-in-shooting-on-historical-market-square-in-krakow/ Sat, 07 Nov 2026 15:40:50 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106484

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Six people have been killed and many more injured after a man opened fire from a moving vehicle in the historic centre of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, today. Police have apprehended the perpetrator.

The interior minister says that the incident is being treated as a terrorist attack, and that preliminary indications suggest the perpetrator had “very radical far-right” views. Police later discovered three further dead bodies in the suspect’s home, who are believed to be his parents and sister.

📌Premier przekazał, że policja, służby specjalne, prokuratura zrobią wszystko, żeby jak najszybciej przekazać informacje opinii publicznej o powodach (strzelaniny – PAP) – powiedział w sobotę na briefingu premier Donald Tusk.

📌- Prawdopodobnie w domu zamachowca są nieżywi… pic.twitter.com/gnV7c1TALa

— Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) November 7, 2026

At around 3 p.m. local time on Saturday, a man who had driven onto Kraków’s market square – a large public space filled with tourists and locals – “began firing at random people from his car”, said police.

They later confirmed that six people – four women and two men – have died and 15 were injured. Three of the deceased have been identified as Polish women, and one other as a British man. The two other victims have not been identified at the time of writing.

The police also revealed that there is only one suspected perpetrator, that he is a Polish citizen, and that he has been detained and transported to hospital.

~aktualizacja
Zmarła kolejna z osób poszkodowanych w zdarzeniu na Rynku Głównym w Krakowie. Na ten moment nie żyje 6 osób. 4 kobiety i 2 mężczyzn. pic.twitter.com/yK6a7fSj2P

— Małopolska Policja (@kwpkrakow) November 7, 2026

Footage from Republika, a TV station that had been present in the city centre to report from an anti-government protest that was taking place today, showed paramedics appearing to treat victims on the square.

The station also broadcast footage showing the car from which shots were fired driving through a street that leads away from the square. A police car can be seen behind it and the apparent sound of gunfire can be heard.

Moment ucieczki czarnego Subaru w Krakowie, widać, że sprawca strzela z samochodu do ludzi… pic.twitter.com/VfWYtx8PYX

— chrzanik (@chrzanikx) November 7, 2026

Further videos and photos shared on social media show the alleged perpetrator being apprehended by a police officer, with both men injured and requiring medical treatment.

The suspect is wearing a military-style uniform, including some kind of helmet and face covering, while what looks like an AR-15-style rifle can be seen on the ground alongside him.

A spokeswoman for provincial police headquarters in Kraków, Katarzyna Cisło, later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that police officers had fired at the suspect, who had returned fire. Two police officers were injured during the incident, with one undergoing surgery and described as being in critical condition.

🔴Strzelanina w Krakowie. Jest nagranie z momentu zatrzymania zamachowca pic.twitter.com/2EXVvLEoRY

— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) November 7, 2026

A spokesman for national police headquarters, Andrzej Fijołek, told TVN that the suspect is a 24-year-old from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a small town in southeastern Poland.

Fijołek revealed that the man has a firearms licence and had used an AR-15 rifle during the incident, which he fired randomly while driving the car. “I can confirm that his attire indicates he was well-prepared, well-armed and knew what he was doing,” he added.

Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced that, contrary to some rumours on social media, the suspect is not and has never been a member of the Polish military.

Stanowczo dementuję informacje pojawiające się w przestrzeni publicznej, że zamachowcem, który dokonał dziś ataku w Krakowie był żołnierz Wojska Polskiego. Mężczyzna nie był i nie jest żołnierzem WP i nigdy nie mial nic wspólnego z wojskiem.

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 7, 2026

On Saturday evening, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński confirmed that “we are dealing with a terrorist attack”. He praised “police officers’ swift response for preventing a much larger massacre”.

Kierwiński said that the perpetrator is currently in critical condition in hospital. He added that the information obtained so far suggests that the attacker had “very, very radical views” and “may have been fascinated by far-right ideologies”.However, the interior minister emphasised that investigations are still ongoing.

Subsequently, Prime Minister Donald Tusk revealed that three further bodies – of two women and one man – had been found at the suspect’s home. He said they were likely his close family members.

Minister @MKierwinski na konferencji w Krakowie: 💬 Sprawca mógł być zafascynowany ideologiami skrajnie prawicowymi. Ten wątek będzie jednak szczegółowo weryfikowany. Czynności prowadzą funkcjonariusze @PolskaPolicja, jak i @ABW_GOV_PL – na miejscu zdarzenia oraz w domu rodzinnym… pic.twitter.com/PppmMPmWYW

— MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) November 7, 2026

Gun violence in Poland is extremely rare, and this kind of mass shooting incident is unheard of. The country also has one of the lowest rates of gun ownership in Europe, though a record number of licences, 50,709, were issued last year.

Kraków is by far Poland’s biggest tourist destination, receiving over 16 million visitors last year. The historic city centre, which is a UNESCO-listed World Heritage Site, would have been filled with locals and tourists on a Saturday afternoon.

A collection of artefacts associated with the Vandals and dating back almost 2,000 years has been handed anonymously to a museum in eastern Poland.

The collection includes a sword, spear and javelin heads, shield components and spurs. Museum staff do not know who originally discovered the burial or exactly where it was located, leaving the circumstances of the find largely a mystery.

The Father Stanisław Staszic Museum in Hrubieszów announced in a Facebook post that the objects had been passed to them anonymously through an intermediary.

The items are in poor condition and will undergo urgent conservation, with the iron components of the weapons particularly vulnerable after centuries in the ground.

They were also exposed to high temperatures during a burial practice in which the deceased was burned along with their personal belongings. The museum says that the nature of the objects indicates that their owner held a high social position.

The most notable object is a sword preserved in three pieces, reflecting the Vandal practice of deliberately breaking or bending weapons and other grave artefacts as part of funeral rituals. The collection also contains two spearheads, both broken.

Other items include a shield boss with a spike, a shield grip, a fragment of a knife, a belt buckle and two spurs. Fragments of a bone comb and a bronze fibula, used to fasten a cloak, were also recovered.

 

The circumstances surrounding the discovery and recovery of the objects remain unknown, but the museum says that, according to the information it has received, the burial site was discovered in an agricultural field several years ago in the municipality of Werbkowice.

“We intend to verify the exact location through archaeological excavations, most likely next summer,” they added. “Based on the information we have gathered, there are strong indications that there may be more similar burials in the area that have been disturbed by agricultural work.”

The opportunity to recover the objects and transfer them to an appropriate institution arose only recently. The museum said that a local metal detectorist played a key role in arranging the transfer, acting as an intermediary in securing the artefacts.

The recovery of the artefacts follows another recent archaeological discovery in the same region. In August, the museum announced that a metal boss from a warrior’s shield dating to the second century was found at a scrap metal yard near Hrubieszów.

The Vandals were an ancient Germanic people believed to have reached the territories of present-day Poland around the 3rd or 2nd century BC.

They lived in the region for several centuries and are generally associated by researchers with the Przeworsk culture, which flourished across parts of present-day Poland during the Iron Age and Roman period.

Around the turn of the 4th and 5th centuries AD, amid the expansion of the Huns, they left Central Europe and moved westwards into the declining Roman Empire. As the Vandals left Central Europe, the Slavic population gradually moved into the region over the following centuries.

Święczkowski denounced the takeover as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence when it ruled from 2015 to 2023.

 

As well as pitting judges aligned with the national-conservative PiS, which is now the main opposition party, and the current more liberal government against one another, the dispute also centres around the legitimacy of certain judges.

The International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) has criticised the takeover of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) by a group of government-backed judges. It says that the move “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”.

However, the ICJ, a Swiss-based NGO led by judges, lawyers and academics from around the world, also chastised Poland’s opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, for his role in the crisis surrounding the TK, in particular his refusal to swear in judges elected by parliament.

🚨#Poland’s constitutional crisis must be resolved through the rule of law. The ICJ urges all authorities to respect judicial independence, follow lawful procedures, and comply with European court rulings.

🔗More information: https://t.co/NWmca9mpUx

— ICJ (@ICJ_org) November 3, 2026

On Friday, eight judges who were elected to the TK this year by the government’s parliamentary majority effectively took over the tribunal. They announced that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to properly fulfil their duties.

Meanwhile, large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the grounds.

Święczkowski denounced the takeover of the court as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the rule of the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence.

Nawrocki has likewise denounced the actions of the government-backed judges. In the early hours of Saturday, he dramatically forced his way into the court, where he clashed physically and verbally with the judges who had taken over the TK.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

In a statement on Tuesday, the ICJ expressed regret that the latest developments have “deepened the crisis over the tribunal”. It called on Polish “state institutions to seek solutions…that comply fully with the rule of law, including the principle of the independence of the judiciary”.

The ICJ’s secretary-general, Santiago Canton, noted that Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of the eight TK judges elected by parliament this year. That “violates international standards and is contrary to the interim measures indicated by the European Court of Human Rights”, said Canton.

In May, the ECHR issued an interim order for all judges elected by parliament to be allowed to serve on the court. However, that has been ignored by Nawrocki and Święczkowski, who argued that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision.

The ICJ also noted that the roots of the crisis at the TK date back a decade, to the time when the PiS government took actions – including unlawfully appointing judges to the tribunal – that rendered the court illegitimate.

 

“At the same time,” continued Canton, “the suspension of the president and vice-president of the tribunal without a fair and appropriate procedure established by law, carried out with the involvement of the police, contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary.”

In its statement, the ICJ added that “criminal and disciplinary proceedings must respect all the guarantees of a fair trial and must never be used as a means to change [a court’s] composition”.

Later on Tuesday, after the ICJ had issued its statement, the eight government-backed judges held their first general assembly, at which they moved forward with disciplinary proceedings against Święczkowski and Sochański.

The justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, has also submitted six requests to the TK to lift Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution so that he can face charges for a range of alleged crimes relating to both his time as chief justice and his previous role as a senior prosecutor under the PiS government.

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 3, 2026

The takeover of the TK has also stirred controversy among Polish legal experts. The issue has even caused an unprecedented split at the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a well-respected NGO.

On Saturday, the HFPC’s management board issued a statement, signed by its president, Maciej Nowicki, saying that it “sees no clear legal basis” for the actions taken on Friday by the government-backed judges to suspend Święczkowski and take control of the tribunal.

It warned that the situation “set a dangerous precedent” and “does not contribute to fixing the tribunal”. However, HFPC also made it clear that the crisis at the court dates back a decade and reiterated its view that Nawrocki “has no right to block or invalidate the election [of judges] by parliament”.

Pełna treść stanowiska: https://t.co/OvJPpaGDel pic.twitter.com/2UpV2itgcd

— Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka (@hfhrpl) October 31, 2026

That statement prompted six of the eight members of HFPC’s council – a separate body from the management board – to resign. Those to depart included a former chief justice of the TK, Andrzej Rzepliński, and a former deputy human rights commissioner, Hanna Machińska.

Machińska announced their resignation in a social media post. She said that the reason for her decision had been the management board’s statement, “with which I disagree”. Speaking later to broadcaster TVN, Machińska said that “we believe that the legal basis [for the TK takeover] was clearly defined”.

Poland’s government, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has also argued that the takeover of the tribunal was necessary to ensure that legally appointed judges can take up their seats and that the court’s legitimacy can be restored.

However, on Tuesday evening, Tusk shifted to a more conciliatory tone, offering to hold a one-on-one meeting with Nawrocki to discuss the crisis around the Constitutional Tribunal and “try to find solutions that will protect Poland from any political upheaval”.

However, the situation is mired in controversy and uncertainty. Święczkowski and the opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, do not recognise the judges who are now claiming control of the court, describing their actions as a “coup d’état”.

For a general assembly of the TK to be valid, two thirds of the court’s judges need to be present. Normally, given that the tribunal has 15 positions, that would mean at least 10 judges being present.

Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. Prices in Poland were also among the fastest-rising in the bloc.

Poland’s relatively high electricity costs reflect the country’s continued reliance on coal, which results in EU charges for carbon emissions, and its taxes and levies, which make up the largest share of household electricity bills anywhere in the EU.

In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. This was the seventh-highest price among the EU’s 27 member states and above the bloc-wide average of €28.32.

Ireland (€38.71 per 100 kWh) had the highest prices, followed by Germany (€36.18) and Belgium (€35.75). The lowest costs were recorded in Hungary (€11.39), Malta (€12.68) and Bulgaria (€13.41).

However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh.

Only Romania had higher prices, at 46.89 PPS. The lowest prices when measured in PPS were recorded in Malta (13.75), Hungary (14.7) and Luxembourg (15.47).

Poland’s electricity prices, in PPS terms, rose by 10.7% compared with the second half of 2025, which was the second-biggest increase in the EU after Finland. They were also up 17.6% compared to the first half of 2025, the fourth-largest rise in the bloc.

 

One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power, by far the highest proportion in the EU.

Almost all coal used in Polish power plants is mined domestically and is among the most expensive in the world to extract. Additionally, burning it also produces high carbon emissions, which power generators must pay for under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS).

These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. This was the highest share in the EU, ahead of Germany (23.6%) and well above the bloc-wide average of 18.6%.

“In Poland, only one-third of our electricity generation is carbon-free. We have to pay for the rest – often dearly,” noted Polish energy journalist Jakub Wiech, commenting on the data.

Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27.

However, Bartłomiej Orzeł of the Project Tempo think tank notes that electricity prices in Poland would, in fact, be even higher were it not for the huge state subsidies paid to support the unprofitable coal mining sector, which amount to billions of zloty a year but also shield end consumers from the full cost of extracting coal.

He told news website Interia that mines actually sell coal to power stations at a price below the cost of extraction.

Poland will from next month be the last remaining EU country still mining hard coal, after the Czech Republic – the only other producer – announced the closure of its last mine https://t.co/0sfMDQb19N

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026

According to Wiech, the high tax burden also reflects the costs of transforming Poland’s energy sector while continuing to support coal-fired power stations and the state budget.

He says Poland needs “on the one hand, to fund the accelerated but delayed transformation and modernisation of the electricity sector; on the other hand, to maintain the fleet of coal-fired power stations; and thirdly, to contribute to the state budget”, which is struggling with persistently high deficits.

Wiech expects, however, that politicians will come under pressure to reduce electricity bills ahead of next year’s parliamentary election. He says they may be tempted to “interfere with electricity bills” and that “it is therefore quite likely that certain charges (e.g. the distribution charge) will be reduced in 2027”.

Komisja Europejska wrzuciła dane o cenach prądu za I półrocze 2026 roku i – boy, oh, boy – niesamowita jest to lektura.

Na początek mocne uderzenie: w ujęciu standardu siły nabywczej polskie gospodarstwa domowe mają drugie najwyższe ceny prądu w całej Unii Europejskiej.… pic.twitter.com/yKvt5251i7

— Jakub Wiech (@jakubwiech) November 1, 2026

Energy prices and the wider energy transition have already become increasingly politicised this year, with the right-wing opposition criticising EU climate policies.

The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, recently called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from ETS, claiming that it treats “Poles as a cash machine for the absurd leftist climate policy of the EU”.

Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has twice attempted to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policy, but in both cases his proposals were rejected by the more pro-EU government’s majority in parliament.

Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026

However, when PiS was in power from 2015 to 2023, it recognised the need to move Poland away from coal and towards a mix of renewables and nuclear.

Solar energy installations boomed under the PiS government, and the overall share of renewables in the energy mix rose from around 9% in 2015 to a record 29% in 2024.

The current government has continued with PiS’s plans to shift towards nuclear and renwables. This year, Poland’s first offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea began generating electricity, with a number of other offshore projects set to follow.

Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%).

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Sun, 08 Nov 2026 18:07:12 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Hiring rate declines in October in ‘end to positive news for jobs’ https://www.cityam.com/hiring-rate-declines-in-october-in-end-to-positive-news-for-jobs/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:01:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2475184

Hiring activity declined in October, reversing momentum in the jobs market over previous months.  Data compiled by a leading industry group showed the number of permanent placements fell last month at the second-fastest pace this year as employers pulled back on hiring.  Vacancies also continued to fall although the drop was the softest in over [...]]]>

Hiring activity declined in October, reversing momentum in the jobs market over previous months. 

Data compiled by a leading industry group showed the number of permanent placements fell last month at the second-fastest pace this year as employers pulled back on hiring. 

Vacancies also continued to fall although the drop was the softest in over two years.

Researchers said the fall in permanent placements, along with the first decline in temporary billings since March, was in part due to a rise in borrowing costs from higher interest rates and energy costs hampering firms. 

KPMG UK chief executive Jon Holt said struggles to deal with costs could further weigh on hiring confidence. 

“October saw employers pull back on hiring in the month leading up to the Budget, ending a run of more positive news over recent months,” Holt said. 

“Businesses will now be assessing whether the measures announced in the Budget give them enough stability to absorb the external pressures and higher costs they face. 

“But with the Bank of England increasing interest rates and inflation set to continue rising over the coming months, there is a risk the green shoots we had been seeing in the jobs market could stall.”

Budget ‘missed opportunity’ for jobs boost

Maxine Bligh, interim chief executive at the REC, said some resilience in hiring across London and the north of England was promising although labelled the Budget a “missed opportunity for both jobs and growth”. 

A slowdown in the jobs market could weaken the case for another imminent interest rate hike, with Bank of England policymakers arguing on Thursday that signs of stabilisation had added to inflationary pressures in the UK economy. 

But the latest official data published by the Office for National Statistics showed vacancy levels dropping below 700,000 for the first time in over five years.

S&P Global data crunched by KPMG and REC researchers suggested that there was increased demand for workers in IT and computing, engineering and construction.

]]> 2475184Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Oxford Street pedestrianisation brings ‘staggering’ shopping boost https://www.cityam.com/oxford-street-pedestrianisation-brings-staggering-shopping-boost/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:01:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2475300

The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street has delivered a “staggering’ boost in footfall, data compiled by the London mayor’s office has shown, as Christmas shopping could usher in a larger surge in the number of shoppers.  Datasets gathered by City Hall suggest that spending and footfall soared in the first week of a traffic-free Oxford Street, [...]]]>

The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street has delivered a “staggering’ boost in footfall, data compiled by the London mayor’s office has shown, as Christmas shopping could usher in a larger surge in the number of shoppers. 

Datasets gathered by City Hall suggest that spending and footfall soared in the first week of a traffic-free Oxford Street, even as the mayor’s decision to close it to buses and cyclists divided Londoners. 

According to City Hall, footfall between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street rose by 16 per cent compared to the October 2025 half-term while international visitor numbers were up by about 42 per cent. 

Visits after 6pm also rose, with researchers arguing that data has far surpassed expectations. Data by the payments company Adyen also suggested that spending at stores down the traffic-free area of Oxford Street grew from £2.9m to £3.7m year-on-year, it was revealed last week. 

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said the results were a “real boost for the nation’s high street”. 

“These are staggering early results that show the transformational impact that the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street will have,” Khan said. 

“With Christmas around the corner, I’d encourage Londoners and visitors to come and see what a traffic-free Oxford Street has to offer, whether you’re here to shop, meet friends or make an evening of it. The new Oxford Street is going to be one of the world’s most exciting public spaces, so come and be a part of this truly momentous project.”

Oxford Street change divides London

The decision to shut off Oxford Street has split Londoners, with cyclists and residents protesting against the mayor’s intervention. 

The Marylebone Association, which is made up of locals living around the area, used public information to argue that bus journeys are taking up to 11 minutes longer following the pedestrianisation. 

Hundreds of cyclists also staged a protest near Oxford Circus over a week ago.  

Khan had pushed for a boost in shopping levels across Oxford Street for years, even as critics have complained about candy shops and other Harry Potter-style gift stores opening over the years. The mayor has argued that the pedestrianisation of the street would encourage “quality shops” to move in, adding that “decline is not inevitable”. 

]]> 2475300Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Nandy flags downsides of closer EU relations https://www.cityam.com/nandy-flags-downsides-of-closer-eu-relations/ Sun, 08 Nov 2026 11:34:37 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2475294

Cabinet minister Lisa Nandy has suggested there are downsides to closer relations with the European Union. Speaking to the BBC, Nandy said she acknowledged there were “trade-offs” from boosting trade with the EU.  The culture secretary, who has a brief overseeing digital and telecommunications sectors, said she did not want to “cut people out of [...]]]>

Cabinet minister Lisa Nandy has suggested there are downsides to closer relations with the European Union.

Speaking to the BBC, Nandy said she acknowledged there were “trade-offs” from boosting trade with the EU. 

The culture secretary, who has a brief overseeing digital and telecommunications sectors, said she did not want to “cut people out of that conversation”. 

“There are trade-offs to be made,” Nandy told the BBC. 

“The only thing that I think the British people are absolutely united on right now is that we left the European Union a decade ago with the promise of a close Brexit deal and the promise of benefits from that deal, and most of those have not been realised.

“It’s not working for people across this country, and we’ve got to do better.”

Her responses came in response to questions about whether there would be a cap on the number of Europeans who would come to Britain under a youth mobility scheme. 

No ‘cherry-picking’ in EU relations

A debate over the terms of negotiations has erupted after Andy Burnham re-iterated he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime. 

Michel Barnier, the former Brexit negotiator for the EU who was later prime minister of France for a short period of time, said the UK would need to accept free movement in order to get further trade access. 

“There is no cherry picking,” he said.

“There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms [of goods, movement of people, services and capital] are clearly the four conditions to be inside the single market.”

Reports have suggested that Sir Keir Starmer was considering a security and customs union framework in negotiations before resigning as Prime Minister in the summer. 

Burnham will meet EU leaders in Dublin this week while a UK-EU summit is scheduled for 20 November. Leaders are expected to sign off deals on energy markets and food standards. 

Reform UK’s Nigel Farage and the Conservatives have hit out at the government over its plans to push ahead with moving closer to the EU, potentially even crossing so-called “red lines” on not joining the customs union or single market in the Labour manifesto from 2024. 

]]> 2475294Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar ‘Dear CEO’: Union reps hit chief executive inboxes at 12.03am https://www.cityam.com/dear-ceo-union-reps-hit-chief-executive-inboxes-at-12-03/ Sun, 08 Nov 2026 11:02:47 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2475291

Union bosses flooded chief executives’ email inboxes at 12.03am, minutes after new workers’ rights rules came into effect, it has been reported.   GMB representatives contacted thousands of company chiefs with a template email starting “Dear CEO” on 30 October, according to the Sunday Times.  The emails reportedly informed bosses of employees’ legal rights to access [...]]]>

Union bosses flooded chief executives’ email inboxes at 12.03am, minutes after new workers’ rights rules came into effect, it has been reported.  

GMB representatives contacted thousands of company chiefs with a template email starting “Dear CEO” on 30 October, according to the Sunday Times. 

The emails reportedly informed bosses of employees’ legal rights to access trade unions. 

GMB is one of the country’s biggest unions and represents hundreds of thousands of workers. Representatives asked to “meet, recruit or organise workers” as soon as legal rights came into effect.

Chief executives were also told about the unions’ right to invite all staff to online meetings which are conducted during work hours. 

The move represents unions’ push to capitalise on new workers rights brought through a new section of e Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992. 

“Each week, the GMB will provide one item of union information (for example, a message, bulletin, short video, poster or link). The employer will distribute it, in full and in a stand-alone format, to all workers,” the email said, according to reports. 

The communication must be delivered over channels that a company “normally uses”, such as by email, intranet, Slack or Microsoft Teams, bosses were told.

Union bosses back ‘common sense reforms’

New workers rights though changes to legislation under the Labour government have divided businesses and trade unions. 

The government had to hold crunch negotiations on day one rights for former employees suing bosses for unfair dismissal, leading to a compromise. 

The Office for Budget Responsibility said in October that the new employment rights act would likely damage hiring levels although it did not come to a full assessment. 

Internal government research also showed that workers preferred access to zero hours contracts.

A spokesperson for GMB said: “Good employers know they have nothing to fear from workers having a voice. Those kicking up a fuss might want to ask themselves why they are so frightened of their own staff having the right to speak to a trade union.

“These common-sense reforms will give people a stronger voice at work. They will help rebalance our economy so that everyone can benefit, not just those at the top.”

]]> 2475291Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Women’s football doesn’t need to become men’s football to succeed https://www.cityam.com/womens-football-doesnt-need-to-become-mens-football-to-succeed/ Sun, 08 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474815

Women’s football is on a continual gradient of growth. The curve has been getting steeper and steeper each year, each season – more investment, more interest, more sales, more TV airtime. However, the investment into the women’s game and player welfare is growing at a slower rate.But as players get older, they gain more responsibility, [...]]]>

Women’s football is on a continual gradient of growth. The curve has been getting steeper and steeper each year, each season – more investment, more interest, more sales, more TV airtime. However, the investment into the women’s game and player welfare is growing at a slower rate.

But as players get older, they gain more responsibility, and it is not currently feasible for all players to be full-time.

Outside of the top clubs players rely on personal sponsorship and branding deals to get by. That may work for players in the WSL but what about players in tiers three and four? How do we bridge the gap between full-time and part-time?

We’ve seen plenty of women’s players become social media influencers and content creators, such as Alisha Lehmann and Kelci Rose Bowers. But what businesses could players get themselves into?

Our Actonians player Lois Colley has recently started her own events coffee bar business. But I’ve been on a different journey – from being paid to play football, to being involved in building businesses outside of the game, to getting trained in high level finance, and also supporting my family’s investment in a football club.

Women’s football needs to address its issues

Today’s players don’t just have to become tomorrow’s coaches or broadcasters. They could become owners, investors, founders, executives and decision-makers. They bring something traditional investors don’t necessarily have: lived experience of the game. 

Women are creators. We don’t need to follow a path that’s already been etched, we can create our own ecosystem that benefits us. 

The differences between men’s and women’s football aren’t just challenges – they’re opportunities. Mary Earps said to “leave the shirt in a better place than it was before”. If we’re not developing the game then what are we doing?

The current roster of players have so much more today than we had at their age. We should absolutely continue to fight for female footballers to be paid what their talent and the growing value of the game deserves. But we shouldn’t allow salary to become the only measure of progress. 

The bigger opportunity is to create an ecosystem in which women don’t just play the game. They build businesses around it, invest in it, own parts of it and ultimately help decide what it becomes.

Women’s football doesn’t need to become men’s football to succeed. It has the opportunity to become something better and create something that suits us.

So let’s expand our thinking and create a future for women’s football in a way nobody has seen before.

Stephanie McCaffrey is an entrepreneur, women’s sport investor and former USA football player.

France Rugby is set to replace Altrad as its front-of-shirt partner. City AM asked industry experts who could get the new gig.

Rugby’s big 10 nations, unsurprisingly, garner much financial support from major commercial deals, with front-of-shirt sponsors the most lucrative source of income.

O2, Vodafone (twice), Vittoria, Altrad (twice), Cadbury and FNB are the big hitters set to feature on kits at rugby’s Nations Championship, which resumes this weekend. But for construction firm Altrad, founded by Syrian-born French resident Mohed Altrad, it will be the last year adorning the front of the famous Les Bleus shirt. 

After nearly a decade the French Rugby Federation this week reportedly signed the document that concluded the partnership, effective July 2027. So who could take over after the Six Nations?

“France has a €10m shirt to sell and a small pool of buyers who can afford it and for whom it would make commercial sense, so the FFR should look beyond rugby’s traditional sponsors,” Laurence Miller of Red Tiger Marketing tells City AM. 

“The brands with the most money moving into European sport right now are Chinese car makers and AI enabled companies.”

Altrad out…

Adds MSQ Sport + Entertainment’s Steve Martin: “I think the greater context is the French team is built around Antoine Dupont – probably the most recognisable rugby player at the moment – and they’ve got that French flair. France’s rugby is a very powerful, well-loved team in the country, so it attracts big dollars and big euros for its partnerships.”

International rugby teams are not allowed commercial partners on their shirts at a World Cup, but whichever brand replaces Altrad will have links with the nation who are among the favourites to lift the trophy in Australia next summer.

England have led the way in commercialising their brand, recently entering into a renewed deal with O2 while adding Lloyds as their first back-of-shirt sponsor and Allianz as stadium naming rights partner.

…shipping in?

“French rugby fans are a third more likely than average to be business decision-makers and 36 per cent more likely to be senior managers,” Miller adds. “That’s exactly who B2B tech, AI and financial services brands are trying to reach.

“Mistral AI, Alan, Qonto and Pennylane all fit that profile, and Pennylane is already sponsoring the Top 14 finals. The winner will most likely be one of the new wave of global brands buying into European sport, or one of France’s emerging tech champions looking to make its name on the world stage.”

Concludes Martin: “You’ve got the 2027 Rugby World Cup looming, which is always a great focal point.

“The market in rugby is up and down for sponsorship generally but internationally the big teams haven’t struggled and they’ve actually had long-term partnerships.

“I think they’ve got something up their sleeve and you’re looking at brands like Orange, Axa, Michelin. There is another brand that’s in the market and that’s the shipping firm CMA CGM – they’re ones to watch.”
