Ambitious Wrexham AFC have named former EFL boss Shaun Harvey the club’s acting CEO following the shock departure of Michael Williamson.

American Williamson has been a key figure in their meteoric rise to the Championship since joining the club – owned by Hollywood duo Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac – in 2024 but has left abruptly. 

“We thank Michael Williamson for his two years at Wrexham and for his work taking the club from League 1 to the Championship,” said Reynolds and Mac.

“Since our takeover five years ago, Wrexham have had historic success on the pitch and won hearts all over the globe. We remain focused on our most important task: to make the Wrexham community proud.

“Shaun Harvey has been an integral part of this journey from the beginning, and we know Shaun will give every support to Phil Parkinson and the lads on the pitch while keeping the broader Wrexham community roaring us on.”

Williamson held senior roles at Inter Milan and in Major League Soccer before joining Wrexham in the summer of 2024 and was named Football Industry Leader of the Year in 2025.

He did not always prove a popular figure with Wrexham fans, however, with news of his sudden exit being welcomed by some on social media. 

How Wrexham’s rise has stalled

No-nonsense Harvey, 56, has worked with Reynolds and Mac since their takeover of then-non-league Wrexham in 2021, first as an advisor and then joining as a director in 2023. 

An experienced football administrator, he was chief executive of the English Football League for six years until 2019, following spells at Leeds United and Bradford City. 

The club’s dizzying ascent, chronicled in the docuseries Welcome To Wrexham, has stalled after three successive promotions carried them from the fifth tier to the second in 2025.

They narrowly missed out on the play-offs last season but have made a mixed start to the new campaign and currently sit 16th in the Championship.

]]> 2475270Frank Dalleres Frank Dalleres UK’s wealthiest financier Michael Platt sues own lawyer for professional negligence https://www.cityam.com/uks-wealthiest-financier-michael-platt-sues-own-lawyer-for-professional-negligence/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:15:59 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2475121

The UK’s wealthiest financier, Michael Platt, and his hedge fund are suing their former lawyer for alleged professional negligence and preparing for a trial. The claim was filed in September last year against Malcolm Gammie KC, a barrister at One Essex Court, following the billionaire and his firm being in a long-running dispute with HMRC [...]]]>

The UK’s wealthiest financier, Michael Platt, and his hedge fund are suing their former lawyer for alleged professional negligence and preparing for a trial.

The claim was filed in September last year against Malcolm Gammie KC, a barrister at One Essex Court, following the billionaire and his firm being in a long-running dispute with HMRC over the tax treatment of earnings on senior traders and partners at Bluecrest under a so-called partner incentivisation plan (PIP).

Gammie, a senior tax barrister, represented Bluecrest, Platt, and Bluecrest’s former chief financial officer and partner, Andrew Dodd, in the First Tier Tribunal in 2017 and then in 2021 at the Upper Tribunal.

When the case reached the Court of Appeal in 2023, the judges ruled that senior traders and partners at the firm must pay income tax on the incentive plan rather than a lower corporation tax rate, which Bluecrest had been paying.

In the judgment, the judge had criticised Gammie’s legal approach, pointing to an analogy which Gammie drew between the PIP incentive plan and a partner who withdraws capital from the partnership and describing it as “not exact” and “apt to mislead.”

In a case management conference on Friday ahead of a trial, the Commercial Court heard issues concerning tax treatment in relation to the incentive plan after Platt’s decision to move the hedge fund’s operational headquarters from London to Geneva in 2010 for tax purposes.

The court also heard issues concerning whether Platt and Dodd’s bank and credit card statements dating back 17 years should be used as evidence in the trial, which Bluecrest’s barrister said would be “both time consuming and could turn into an expensive wild goose chase.”

The trial is expected to assess whether Gammie acted negligently by not advising Platt and Dodd to use Swiss tax residency arguments during the legal dispute with HMRC, and whether this led to “a lost opportunity” to pursue different arguments, Bluecrest’s barrister said.

He added that if the documents “can be found, perhaps there will be thousands of pages, which might mean the defendant could make intrusive inquiries” about other things.

Judge Mr Justice Stanley told the court the documents “should be included” but said “it will require careful thought to be given on how the bank statements are disclosed and how they are deployed if they are to be deployed in a public trial”.

Members of an LLP, a structure Bluecrest uses, are treated as self-employed partners, meaning they don’t pay the 15 per cent employer’s national insurance contributions on their pay.

HMRC taking ‘aggressive’ stance on LLPs

This comes after a separate landmark ruling in July in which the UK’s Supreme Court ruled against the hedge fund run by Platt, finding that partners in a Limited Liability Partnership (LLPs) must be taxed as employees rather than as self-employed profit-sharers. Bluecrest now faces a near £200m tax bill as a result of the ruling.

The judge unanimously rejected BlueCrest’s argument that its partners were technically self-employed and therefore not subject to the same income tax and national insurance as normal employees.

The ruling sent shock-waves through the professional services sector, whom the vast majority use the LLP structure, raising concern over whether it would leave them liable to pay hefty tax bills to HMRC.

City AM has since revealed the UK tax authority is actively writing to limited liability partnerships (LLPs) as firms race to reassess their members’ tax status after the landmark legal ruling, even as both sides “hold their cards close to their chests.”

Gammie and HMRC declined to comment. BlueCrest was contacted for comment.

The trial date is yet to be decided.

]]> 2475121Rosie Harris-Davison Rosie Harris-Davison Wales rugby in death spiral but fans snubbing Principality won’t help https://www.cityam.com/wales-rugby-in-death-spiral-but-fans-snubbing-principality-wont-help/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474854

It’s that time of year again: when Wales try and win a game of rugby while thousands of fans boycott matches at their Principality Stadium. There are thousands and thousands of tickets still available for Wales’ three autumn fixtures in the inaugural Nations Championship finals month. They take on Japan this weekend before matches against [...]]]>

It’s that time of year again: when Wales try and win a game of rugby while thousands of fans boycott matches at their Principality Stadium.

There are thousands and thousands of tickets still available for Wales’ three autumn fixtures in the inaugural Nations Championship finals month.

They take on Japan this weekend before matches against southern hemisphere giants New Zealand and Australia. It could spell millions in lost revenue for the Wales Rugby Union. But can you blame the fans?

It looked as if the side were on the up, defeating Italy and Fiji as well as the Barbarians between March and July. But then the men in red were well beaten in Argentina and spanked by world champions South Africa in Durban. It’s left fans feeling like the side are back to where they were when they endured a 17-game winless run.

Wales excuses?

But that’s no excuse. The Welsh Rugby Union is in crisis, the future of the regional game is in crisis and their best players are flocking across the River Severn and thriving in Prem Rugby. Investment often looks misplaced and badly targeted. Something needs to give.

But what cannot happen is fans turning their noses up at tickets to watch the national team, missing the chance for youngsters to be inspired to get into the game – even if that is through a fixation on how good New Zealand are rather than how poor Wales have been.

Welsh rugby columnist Paul Williams this week said: “I genuinely cannot think of a quicker way to ensure that Welsh rugby is guaranteed to move to two or three regions than to stop buying tickets for Wales games. Those tickets literally fund the game in Wales at all levels. Mind bending.”

State of the game

He’s bang on. But Wales must give their fans something worth dipping hands in very tight pockets for. It is not the easiest time at the moment and I can take my kids to the cinema for the price of one ticket to see Wales take on Australia.

People will rightly bemoan the price of tickets in London, too, but England have managed to virtually sell out every fixture this autumn – against the same trio of teams Wales are facing. And that’s despite needing to sell three days of rugby in this month’s fourth and final weekend – which will feature 12 teams with fixtures confirmed at just a week’s notice.

The point is this: Wales are in a hole. Fans don’t want to watch a losing team, a losing team is bad for business, and bad revenues impact the game and fans you rely on to turn up. It’s a death spiral and someone needs to break the chain. The quick fix is a good autumn. No pressure.

A rout in AI and tech stocks has wiped trillions off global markets. For City AM’s Midday Markets newsletter, Ali Lyon chews over what it all means.

It’s been one of those mornings when analysts have woken up and reached for their morbid bon mots of choice. “Bloodbath” has proven popular. So too, “capitulation-level event” or “sea of red”. And others have simply opted for an unadorned: “extraordinary.”

Whatever one’s preferred descriptor, there is only one markets story on town this Friday: the historic, tech-driven sell-off afoot in global markets, and whether the AI revolution has gone from boom, to bubble, to crash.

Before we get into why this is happening, and what it might all mean, it’s worth reflecting on the events that led us here. It all started, really, when traders began to digest the consequences of this week’s US midterms.

As well as the cost of living – not to mention voters’ enormous misgivings at the Trump administration’s unapologetic cronyism – data centers were firmly on the ballot this Tuesday. And as the ‘blue-nami’ swept through the world’s largest economy, it was clear the scale of the Democrats’ win would presage a slowdown in America’s AI infrastructure rollout.

At US market open on Thursday, the Nasdaq and New York’s S&P 500 fell four per cent and three per cent respectively.

And since then, contagion has well and truly set in, with tech-heavy Asian stock markets all notching up serious falls. The Nikkei – Japan’s blue-chip index – dropped over six per cent while we were all asleep. As did Korea’s Kospi, which has become a bellwether for AI sentiment and was forced to halt trading amid liquidity concerns.

In all, trillions have been wiped off global stock markets, in a rout that has led some investors openly to speculate whether the artificial intelligence boom that has defined the past few years in markets is now firmly in reverse.

What does the AI sell-off mean?

There are, in my mind, three big things worth noting in and among all this. First is that, while today’s rout is striking in its severity, it by no means represents a sudden or drastic change.

Tech stocks – particularly those most exposed to the furthest excesses of AI exuberance – have been on a downward trend for much of the past couple of months.

Companies like Sandisk – which makes memory chips for data centers – may have fallen by 22 per cent yesterday, but that fall was itself off the back of a 45 per cent drop in the preceding month-and-a-bit. And most of the the so-called hyperscalers – Nvidia, Meta, Alphabet and Tesla – are all trading considerably down on the start of the year.

Second, even if this is the start of a period of protracted share price falls, it would by no means herald the end of the AI boom at large. Firms and individuals are still adopting the technology at a rate of knots – and the productivity boom derived from it is by no means jeopardised by today’s shift in market sentiment.

Think back to the dotcom bubble of the early noughties. Investors got well ahead of their skis then, too. Pets.com – the poster child of worldwide web enthusiasm – reached peak valuation of $400m despite only ever generating $5m in revenue and losing over $60m a year. But its overdue crash did not stop the internet becoming the defining innovation of its time, nor slow folks’ adoption of it.

One thing that is certainly worth keeping an eye on though – the final element of the three – is what it may mean for the US and global economies. There is an understandable view in some quarters that the fate of the stock market is dislocated from that of the real economy: that Wall Street and Main Street don’t interact as much as one might think. But – and this is especially true in the US – the ‘wealth effect’ as it is known is a powerful thing.

If people look at their pension pot or stocks and shares Isa over here – or their individual retirement account the US – and they see it looking healthy, they’re more likely to buy that car for which they have been pining, or go our for that indulgent dinner. But when it looks less rosy, as will be the case today, then the opposite is true. Demand consequently slows, and economies grind to a halt.

All of which, is a very long-winded way of saying, there’s a lot going on in AI and markets at the moment. And no-one, least of all me, can say for certain where we’ll find ourselves next.

Must every project justify itself in pounds, shillings and pence? Sizewell C critics are missing the point, writes Charlotte Nichols 

In the depths of the Second World War, John Maynard Keynes took to the airwaves to talk about the importance of rebuilding when peace was achieved. It was 1942 and – despite the crippling impact on public finances – he railed against the “vile doctrine” that every project must justify itself in “pounds, shillings and pence”.

Fast forward to today and – in the realm of energy policy – his point remains. This week parts of Westminster have been scrutinising our nuclear ambitions, and they have failed to see the bigger picture. 

The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) produced a report on the finances that underpin Sizewell C. However, the report – published on the morning of the Budget – misses a key point: reality. It is comparing Sizewell C to a counterfactual deal which was never on the table. And one which would have scared away investors and resulted in yet more delays. The real choice was never about this deal or a perfect alternative. It was between this deal or no power station at all. 

After years of dither and delay, it took a Labour government to get things moving again. Making decisions that will live beyond the next election cycle and improve the lives of our children, and their children. 

And it’s about time too. Because the country has been exposed to global gas prices, which have skyrocketed. Families across the country have seen their monthly bill rise by 58 per cent since the war in Ukraine, and the Iran conflict is pushing them up further still. We are at the whim of events miles away, with no ability to control them. That is a bad deal for the British people. 

The opportunities of Sizewell C

Sizewell is a generational chance to change that for good. Once it’s up and running it will provide homegrown power for 6m homes for at least 60 years. The forecasters reckon it will save the energy system about £2bn a year in the process. 

Obviously, it comes with a cost, and during construction it will put around £1 a month on your bill. But this type of funding model – known as the regulated asset base (RAB) model – actually reduces the cost of financing and, therefore, the cost of electricity.  

When you consider the choice between volatile gas prices and cheaper abundant nuclear power that we control – I think we know which is the better deal. 

And Sizewell is already paying back to society and the economy. The Bank of England’s unanimous decision to raise interest rates to four per cent reflects serious concerns over persistent inflation, not just external shocks. The government most now address root cost issues rather than blaming external factors like the war in Iran, says Emmanuel Igwe

The war in Iran has been central to the Bank of England’s considerations around interest rates for the most of this year. In September, only three of the nine members of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted to raise rates. But this changed this week as, for the first time since August 2023, all nine members voted to increase the Bank Rate. Although eight members supported the rise from 3.75 to four per cent, Catherine Mann wanted the Rate increased to 4.25 percent. The Bank settled on an increase to four percent.

This decision does not come as much of a surprise to the markets, though the unanimity was unexpected. Economists had expected a seven-two split, with those not voting for an increase assumed to support a hold. A unanimous vote reveals something important: the Bank does not consider energy shocks to be a temporary blip. During the press conference, the Bank admitted that, although the shock has not yet passed through to wider wages and prices, it did not want to sit idle and wait until it does.

Central bankers typically overlook temporary supply shocks such as increases in oil prices as they only lead to a one-time increase in the price level, not persistent inflationary pressures. More concerning are second-round effects, such as businesses raising prices to protect profit margins and workers asking for increased wages to keep up with the rising cost of living. 

Running hot

CPI inflation was up from 3.1 in August to 3.5 percent in September, driven mostly by rising fuel prices. 68 per cent of businesses in the Bank’s October Decision Maker Panel said that energy shocks are behind their intentions to raise prices. The OBR expects inflation to peak at 3.75 percent early next year. The forecast from the Bank, released today, shows a gloomier prospect: a rise in inflation of up to five per cent by mid-2027.

In addition to this, the economy is running hot. It is welcome news that Britain was the fastest growing economy in the G7 in the first half of this year. But this is a low bar, and even our modest growth has been met with knock-on price effects from global energy trade. This creates an environment in which businesses pass rising costs to shoppers through raising prices. The Bank says this affected its decision to increase interest rates.

Impact on households will vary. For those with tracker mortgages, payments will go up immediately, while lenders will pass on interest rate increase to those with variable rates within a month. Those with a fixed mortgage rate will be initially insulated from the rate increase but will face a sharp payment increase when their current deal ends and they must remortgage. In a rare bit of good news, those with cash savings, such as prospective first-time buyers, would finally earn a bit of interest after a long while.

Businesses will perhaps suffer more. Firms already shouldering inflated energy bills due to the Iran war now have to contend with higher borrowing costs. Small businesses heavily reliant on variable-rate credit lines and overdrafts will feel it first. This will cast a shadow on the business investment that was the catalyst for Britain’s economic growth this year. Markets are pricing in the prospect for up to four more quarter-rate rises by the end of 2027. If this persists, businesses will see their profits squeezed well into next year. 

To the Treasury, the Bank’s decision was a verdict on the Chancellor’s first Budget. With a fiscal headroom of £15bn – down from £23.6bn recorded in March – the OBR estimated that higher than expected inflation would add £14bn a year to government borrowing costs this parliament. If markets expect a long run of rate rises, debt interest will eat into whatever buffer the Treasury has left.

Critics such as the New Economics Foundation call today’s decision “an act of economic self-harm”. But to hesitate at this moment would be fatal. When a central bank hesitates to act when businesses are signalling to raise prices, it risks losing a grip on market expectations. By raising rates today, it limits the intensity of rate hikes later. Higher interest rates may cool domestic demand, but they cannot lower energy prices or open the Strait of Hormuz. 

Things may change.Energy prices fell after the US midterms this week in an expectation of de-escalation in Iran. Governor Andrew Bailey was careful not to promise more rises. For those in the committee who were doveish such as Alan Taylor and Swati Dhingra, today’s decision was more of an insurance than a firm belief that we are stuck here.

The job now falls to the government to tame supply-driven inflation. Yet the current Treasury strategy features a £4bn sticking plaster that consists partly of a £100 energy rebate that does nothing to alter the trajectory of CPI – shaving only a negligible 0.1 percentage point. The Chancellor must confront the root problems: inflated energy costs, much of which has nothing to do with Iran. He could begin by removing green and social levies from household bills. According to Prosperity Institute research, green initiatives are already set to increase bills by the equivalent of £1,400 per household by 2031. An EU summit looms on 20th November, where Andy Burnham’s proposed UK-EU alignment on carbon costs could just make matters worse. The public might accept pinning the blame on Iran this time round, but neither the Bank nor the government can get away with it indefinitely.

Emmanuel Igwe is an economist at the Prosperity Institute

    HMRC’s upcoming new powers, which allow it to recover tax debts directly from bank accounts, raises questions about how the taxman calculates debt.

    The new powers, unveiled by Chancellor John Healey in the Budget, effective from July 2029, will allow HMRC to automatically deduct debts from holders who fail to engage with the taxman despite being able to pay.

    The powers extend to tax debts up to £5,000 for current and savings accounts, and up to £10,000 for companies. Under the current direct recovery of debts rules, HMRC can take money directly from accounts only if the debt is over £1,000, provided at least £5,000 remains in the accounts.

    This is Labour’s latest move to close Britain’s tax gap. The difference between tax owed and collected stands at £59.2bn in the 2024/25 tax year. The government estimated that the new powers will help raise £50m within the first year, £255m in 2030/31 and £320m in 2031/32.

    James Kipping, head of private client at MHA, said that despite HMRC proposing protections for vulnerable taxpayers, there should be “genuine concern” over how it concludes the debt amount is correct and final, and how it may “distinguish refusal to engage from inability to engage” from taxpayers.

    Kipping also highlighted concerns about what data HMRC uses to determine income and affordability, and how quickly a taxpayer can halt the process and get the money back if HMRC gets it wrong.

    “The significant development is the proposed creation of something approaching an HMRC-imposed payment plan, with the department determining affordability and then causing recurring payments to be extracted from the taxpayer’s account,” Kipping added.

    Compliant taxpayers unlikely to be affected

    Ministers have previously expressed concerns that the high threshold has led to the wide gap, as taxpayers choose to deliberately ignore HMRC demands knowing the taxman is unlikely to chase them. Pursuing debts can also be lengthy and expensive.

    “Most compliant taxpayers are unlikely to be affected, but the success of the measure will depend on robust safeguards and ensuring it is used proportionately where debts are undisputed, and other recovery options have been exhausted,” Rachel Nutt, tax partner at MHA, said.

    “Given we often end up in debates with HMRC that they believe a notice has been sent by them, and yet neither us (as agent) nor the client will have received a copy, it is a cause for concern,” Nutt added.

    London is used to change, transforming from a Roman settlement into a global financial centre.

    The GLA’s draft London Plan gives a good indication of what’s next for the capital – setting out a vision for a city that will be greener and denser by 2050.

    But what does this really mean for the Square Mile – already one of the densest areas of London, defined by sky-high towers rather than leafy parks?

    As the economic powerhouse of the UK, growth within the City should not be constrained if London is to remain globally competitive. Retaining and attracting businesses through swanky new development is important, but the draft Plan doesn’t shy away from the fact this must be balanced with the need for the Square Mile to adapt to a changing climate.

    Time for planners and architects to get creative.

    Temperatures rising

    London is bracing itself for regular 40C heatwaves by 2050, and the iconic glass skyscrapers that dominate the skyline will bear the brunt of our sweltering summers. Conventional air conditioning can act as an easy fix, but the draft London Plan makes it clear that we need to be doing more to ensure our buildings are fit for the future. 

    Part of the solution can be provided at street level. The Square Mile lacks the open land and undeveloped fringes of most London boroughs, so meeting targets for wildlife corridors and urban greening will require an integrated approach that builds nature into London’s streets and rooftops. 

    Think more tree-lined cycle lanes, pocket parks breaking up pavements and living walls on skyscrapers. Increasing green infrastructure across London, including tree canopy and planting, would create cool microclimates around buildings that offer a respite from the hot summers while improving air quality and enhancing biodiversity.  

    Stantec saw the impact of this firsthand in Denver while designing the public realm along the iconic 16th Street. The project introduced over 200 trees made up of 10 different species, supported by an innovative pavement and soil system that provided more than twenty times the amount of uncompacted soil typically available to urban trees.

    Through using public areas to make Denver’s commercial heart more resilient to climate change, one of the city’s most well-known streets has had its economic resilience strengthened too, becoming more vibrant and welcoming for all users – an ambition the Square Mile shares.

    Solutions in the sky

    To fully meet the Plan’s requirements, we also need to be looking up to the City’s skyline – allowing skyscrapers to take on the role of trees in an urban forest.

    This is a challenge faced by cities around the world, and examples from global financial and commercial hubs show you don’t have to choose between density and climate resilience. In fact, future economic strength will increasingly depend on climate resilience – proving that growth, climate adaptation and world-class commercial development can be one side of the same coin.

    Singapore’s Marina One offers an example of climate resilient office buildings, with glass surfaces broken up by green terraces and planting that reduces exposure to the sun and cools the surrounding air. Closer to home, the renovation of the former HSBC tower in Canary Wharf shows how landscaped terraces and retrofitting can enable us to develop more sustainably, with the scheme set to become one of the world’s largest low-carbon office transformations.

    A city facing new extremes

    These greener buildings don’t just help with the heat. In our famously wet country, they also have a role to play in managing rain and more inclement weather. 

    The draft London Plan sets out how new developments must contribute to reducing London’s flood risk, including by using features like green roofs and rain gardens to hold rainwater before it can gradually drain away. 

    Solutions like Denver’s pavement system and Singapore’s hanging gardens directly support this while making the cities more visually appealing too.

    By promoting this approach, the draft Plan offers a glimpse into a future where development is increasingly judged on climate resilience, as well as commercial value.

    The City’s ability to adapt is what has made it one of the most enduring financial hubs in the world.  To ensure we are adequately equipped to grasp the opportunities the next chapter presents, it must be ready to evolve again.

    Greg Pitt is planning director at Stantec

    California has rejected wealth taxes in referendum in a referendum where the ‘no’ campaign was largely funded by self-interested billionaires. It’s the right result for the wrong reason, says Kristian Niemietz

    The final results are not in yet, but unless the remaining uncounted votes are wildly out of the tune with the counted ones, California’s wealth tax proposal has been defeated at the ballot box. 

    ‘Proposition 40’ would have meant a one-off tax of five per cent on net wealth above a threshold of $1bn, payable by people who were residents of California in the beginning of 2026, meaning that leaving the state in order to avoid the tax would not be an option. 

    For those of us who are critical of the current wealth tax fad, though, this referendum victory could be a poisoned chalice, emboldening supporters rather than discouraging them. The opposition may win the referendum, but lose the political narrative. 

    California is home to about 260 billionaires, and the No side in the referendum relied heavily on donations from them, or more precisely, a prominent subset of them. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone contributed over $100m to the campaign. Additional donations from reasonably well-known super-rich people brought the total campaign budget up to about $300m, which enabled them to easily out-spend the pro side by a ratio of almost ten to one. 

    In one sense, the reliance on billionaire support is wholly unsurprising. Suppose you think wealth taxes are a bad idea, and you want to run a campaign against them. Who do you ask for financial support? Of course that’s going to be the people who have both the money to support your campaign, and an obvious interest in doing so. The average Joe is not going to spend money on preventing the introduction of a tax that they will never pay. Sure, opponents will argue that the economic cost of a wealth tax will ultimately fall on the average Joe, not just – or even primarily – on the billionaires who make the transfer to the tax office. But that argument will not be remotely obvious to most people: it takes a lot of explaining, and in order to explain it, you need to be able to finance a campaign first. You are not running a year-long education campaign about tax incidence, second-order effects and unintended consequences. 

    However, while convenient in the short term, opposing wealth taxes in this way comes at a long-term cost. By relying so heavily on the support of people who have an obvious financial self-interest in opposing wealth taxes, you contribute to the impression that financial self-interest is the only reason why someone could possibly oppose wealth taxes. In that way, you play into the hands of their most populist proponents. 

    Slopulism

    I have debated wealth taxes multiple times over the past 18 months or so, on TV, on the radio, at university debating societies. I have found that different people support wealth taxes for very different reasons, and in different ways. The more fair-minded supporters will accept that there are serious, legitimate economic arguments against them. It is just that they – and this is where we differ – do not see this as a reason for abandoning the idea altogether. For them, it is just a reason to be ultra-careful in the design of a wealth tax, and to get the details right. 

    Polanski-style slopulists, on the other hand, refuse to debate in such terms. They will tell a story in which modern politics is a battle between The People, who are good and pure, and The Billionaires, who are rapacious, extractive and divisive. The Billionaires impoverish The People, and then they engage in a divide-and-rule strategy, using their obscene wealth to distort public debate, and foment Hate And Division among The People. In that version of events, economic arguments are just disguised class interests. If you oppose wealth taxes, you must be either a plutocrat defending your ill-gotten gains, or you must be a mercenary in their pay. 

    If I tried to peddle a story along those lines, I would treat the California referendum as a godsend. Had Proposition 40 won, its supporters would now have to deal with the practicalities of a wealth tax, and in due course, with a backlash from disappointed campaigners. Now, the Polanskiites will interpret the result as just another example of billionaires subverting democracy. They will interpret the very defeat of the wealth tax as an illustration of why a wealth tax is necessary in the first place. 

    That’s why, as a critic of wealth taxes, I have to admit that I almost wish the other side had won. 

    Dr Kristian Niemietz is the outgoing editorial director of the Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA). He is the author of the report ‘Fool’s Gold: The case against the wealth tax, and suggestions for alternatives’.

    The Conservatives are on the hunt for their candidate for the London mayor elections in 2028. Mauricio Alencar spoke to one Sir James Cleverly’s challengers, Festus Akinbusoye.

    Festus Akinbusoye imagines what a London under his leadership would look like: outdoor cinemas set up by London’s beauty spots,  thousands more police officers on the streets, celebrities travelling in to make appearances at events, X Games at Trafalgar Square, cranes spotted around the capital building homes, and business booming. 

    It’s a warm vision for a Tory councillor who was only elected into office in May this year. Akinbusoye would have to overcome multiple obstacles in order to make that dream come true. He has just a matter of weeks to convince Tory members in the capital to back him over the political heavyweight, and party favourite, Sir James Cleverly, to run for London mayor. Should he become the Tory candidate, Akinbusoye would then have to get his profile out to Londoners and beat the incumbent Sir Sadiq Khan, or a well-known Labour successor candidate such as David Lammy, Steve Reed or Dawn Butler. 

    Still, Akinbusoye is unfazed. Speaking in early October, he says he is “authentically me”. He is not a conventional politician unlike his competitors he has “lived a lot of life”. Akinbusoye came to London when he was 13 and was Bedfordshire’s police and crime commissioner for three years, holding an equivalent role that the London mayor has for the capital through the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC). He says he has experience as an entrepreneur, starting a company at the age of 16. And, he stresses at multiple times in a half-hour discussion, he is the “most fun, without question”. 

    “Just based on the feedback that I’m getting from members, there is no doubt in my mind that there is a very, very sizeable number of members who want something different, who want a fresh face, who want a break from the past in the sense that Kemi [Badenoch] is talking a lot more now about a new Conservative Party, a changed Conservative party, renewal.”

    Akinbusoye does not spare his superlatives. He will be “most pro-house building mayor London has ever had”, the “most pro-policing”, the “most pro-business”, the “most pro-fun”, the candidate with a “boundless optimism for this great city”. So far, he has published a mini manifesto under the banner “A London Yes Plan” that looks to use government levers to grant housing starts across the capital. 

    ‘Vertical drinking’ battles

    The title of being the “most pro-fun” candidate is not easily tagged onto sitting Westminster councillors. The local authority has come under significant pressure over its proposed rules on “vertical drinking”, out-of-touch legalese for standing up while having a pint, in Soho following reporting in The Guardian, City AM and multiple other newspapers. The draft policy states that venues which provide seated dining spots will get priority in obtaining new licences, on the grounds that it could reduce drunkenness. Critics of the proposal also hit out at the ‘cumulative impact zone’, which extends across a busier part of central London, and forces businesses to abide by stricter licensing rules. 

    Akinbusoye said it was up to Parliament to change rules on licensing objectives. He also argued that “nothing much has changed” and added that most applications that got to a licensing committee, on which he sat, were approved. Many new venues carve out areas for dining with table service. Khan has accused councillors in Westminster of being “arrogant”, to which Akinbusoye says: “The irony is that we’d had a Labour run council up until 2024 in Westminster. He has never raised that issue.”

    Later on, Akinbusoye makes sure to show he drinks while standing up, and that he fully approves of “vertical drinking”. Tory councillors have posted themselves drinking at pubs while standing up on social media – even if the current rules do discourage business owners from allocating more space to standing boozers. 

    He then says that the main problem facing businesses in London is not licensing rules, but rather costs. 

    “I am a very pro-growth, pro-investment, pro-infrastructure person,” he says after speaking about high energy costs, business rates and employment costs. 

    When asked what power the mayor has to reduce costs for businesses, Akinbusoye reflects that they have “convening powers” and “lobbying powers”. He puts this above the powers that mayor has over City Hall’s budget and “soft power” in representing London. If Khan has got one thing right, Akinbusoye suggests, it’s his campaign to get the government to consider re-introducing relief on VAT shopping for tourists. 

    “Probably, that’s a good use of that power,” he says. “But I still go back to where I started, that the biggest concern and the biggest burden that the hospitality industry faces right now is hardly licensing in Westminster.”

    Festus’ vision for leveraging devolution

    Akinbusoye bucks a trend among many mayoral candidates in suggesting he would not want to take all the funding provided by Andy Burnham under prospective devolution plans. The Labour government is expected to announce plans on how a share of income tax generated locally will be kept by metro mayors across the country. Akinbusoye said he wanted at least 50 per cent of those receipts to be used by local authorities so that councillors could deal with “local priorities”. 

    “You would have thought that somebody who wants to be the mayor of London, I want to have all the money and all the power to myself so I can do more. But when we start to extract benefits of wealth from the local people that they create, it’s going to cause a problem in the long run. It doesn’t make sense.”

    Devolution is one issue that Akinbusoye looks ready to take a more unorthodox approach on. Others, such as the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street, he will leave to the past. 

    “There would be absolutely no point in really digging into that now. It’s gonna happen,” he says as he bats away questions about whether he supports the plan. 

    “There’s really no point. It’s like saying ‘what about Brexit’, right? Okay. It’s happened. The thing is, we need to see the data, and the Mayor is transparent about it.”

    The Conservatives in London are edging closer to a decision on who could take on Labour and Reform UK for London. London party members will decide on their preferred candidate by late November. The third candidate is Sara Gezdari.

    At the Tory conference, the likes of Cleverly and Akinbusoye looked to woo activists and relevant members with speeches and engagements. While Akinbusoye may yet surprise Cleverly, he appears to be building a political career backed by younger party members and some former MPs.

    The Tories may still struggle to win London back by 2028. He believes the party needs a candidate that “is going to have the lowest level of voter resistance”.

    While he wants to stand for the party and not as an independent, Akinbusoye appears to maintain a certain level of distance from the Conservatives.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing. An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. Sellers put their concern with being a decent person at 4.99, and buyers guessed 3.78. Buyers put the seller’s interest in money at 6.03; sellers reported 5.06.

The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

]]> Quote of the day: “Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself” https://siliconcanals.com/d-quote-of-the-day-sometimes-you-find-yourself-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-and-sometimes-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-you-find-yourself/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:39 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109380

What happens when your plans collapse, your phone dies, and you're stranded at a gas station thousands of miles from home—and it's the best thing that could've happened.]]>

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.
