]]> Candi Solar, a Swiss clean energy company distributing solar solutions, announced a €44 million ($50 million) financing partnership to build rooftop, ground-mounted, and open-access solar installations paired with BESS across key business hubs in India.

This facility from Pentagreen Capital will enable the avoidance of an estimated 397,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually.

The strategy is also backed by the FAST-P Office under the Monetary Authority of Singapore, Export Finance Australia, International Finance Corporation, the Dutch Entrepreneurial Development Bank (FMO), HSBC, Temasek, British International Investment, Bank of the Philippine Islands, Allied Climate Partners, DBS and Cathay United Bank.

Fabio Eucalipto, co-founder and Director of Candi Solar, said: “Millions of smaller businesses power India’s economy and drive its industrial growth. These companies should benefit from clean, reliable energy without the burden of mastering energy complexities or making major capital commitments.

“At Candi, we have spent years building a customer-first model to make this possible. By combining rooftop and ground-mounted open-access solutions with flexible financing, we can deliver tailored energy solutions at scale.”

Candi Solar’s financing comes amid several 2026 European funding announcements involving renewable-energy infrastructure and commercial battery storage.

In Switzerland, enshift raised €18.5 million to expand integrated energy-transition services, while Germany’s encosa secured €25 million for battery storage targeting SMEs and Feldwerke obtained a €12 million facility for solar project construction.

Elsewhere, Belgium’s Octave.energy raised €10 million and Denmark’s Reel secured €15 million.

Together with Germany’s Einklang (€2.2 million) and Switzerland’s LightSeeds (€162k), these seven selected announcements represent approximately €82.9 million in financing, rising to €126.9 million including Candi Solar’s new €44 million facility.

Marat Zapparov, CEO of Pentagreen Capital added: “India’s growing energy demand and need to reduce oil imports make the transition to clean energy both a strategic and an economic priority. Pentagreen Capital, under Singapore’s FAST-P initiative, is honoured to partner with Candi, whose flexible solar and storage solutions are tailored to the needs of India’s SMEs. Together, we are unlocking finance for projects that make clean energy accessible to an underserved segment, help businesses stabilise their energy costs, and strengthen India’s energy security.”

Founded in 2018 in Zurich, Candi Solar is a clean energy platform that finances, builds, and operates solar and battery storage solutions specifically for commercial and industrial (C&I) businesses, with a particular focus on underserved SMEs. The company looks to mitigate grid instability, lower electricity costs, and accelerate decarbonisation in highly carbon-intensive emerging markets – primarily India and South Africa.

Under Candi’s turnkey shared-value model, clients preserve their capital, paying only for the clean energy generated while Candi manages all engineering, construction and long-term operational performance.

Today’s transaction will finance approximately 400MWp of solar and battery energy storage projects in India, expanding access to clean energy for SME segment, which the company says is underserved with renewable energy access but accounts for 31% of the country’s Gross Domestic Product and 35% of its manufacturing output.

The facility will finance rooftop, ground-mounted, and open-access solar installations paired with BESS across key business hubs in India. These projects are expected to deliver 560 gigawatt hours (GWh) of renewable energy annually, supporting the decarbonisation of 227 commercial and industrial customers, 78% of which are SMEs. This would enable the avoidance of an estimated 397,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually.

Together with recent additional shareholder commitments and an equity round planned for early next year, the capital will help the company accelerate towards installing more than 1 GW of operational solar capacity within the next 24 months – more than doubling its total capacity.

The post Bioliberty raises €2.95 million to bring its AI-powered rehabilitation technology into the home appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Bioliberty, an Edinburgh- and Boston-based rehabilitation technology startup, has raised a €2.95 million ($3.3 million) Series A extension, bringing its total funding to €12.07 million ($13.5 million).

The Series A extension adds four new institutional backers: TGH Ventures, the investment arm of Tampa General Hospital; Ballad Ventures; Belfast-based Whiterock; and 25m Health. The extension builds on the €9.12 million ($10.2 million) previously raised through pre-Series A and Series A rounds.

“This funding and our new strategic investors are crucial to our next phase: creating a more connected rehabilitation journey.  We want to connect data across the patient journey, extend our technology into the home, and use AI to further augment therapy and assessment for physical and occupational therapists,” said Rowan Armstrong, co-founder and CEO, Bioliberty.

Bioliberty was founded in 2020 by Armstrong, Ross O’Hanlon, Conan Bradley, and Shéa Quinn, who hail from Northern Ireland. The company develops soft-robotic rehabilitation technology focused on upper-extremity recovery, primarily targeting patients who have suffered strokes or other mobility-limiting neurological conditions.

Its product suite is made up of three components: Lifehub, a portable control centre that powers the system and delivers interactive therapy sessions; Lifeglov, a soft robotic wearable glove powered by air that assists patients in opening and strengthening their hands; and Lifemind, a clinician-facing dashboard that centralises therapy data and uses AI to auto-generate clinical notes. Lifehub and Lifeglov are FDA-listed in the United States, where Bioliberty launched commercially in 2025.

Bioliberty says its technology was co-developed with leading inpatient rehabilitation facilities, enabling therapy sessions to begin in under five minutes and allowing patients to complete more repetitions per session.

“Bioliberty has been implemented by our therapists seamlessly. Patients are excited to see gains in their function and enjoy the interactivity of the tasks and games they can access,” said Ethan Clark, Therapy Manager, Methodist Rehabilitation Hospital.

For Bioliberty, the Series A extension will support three major priorities: extending its technology into the home environment, connecting rehabilitation data across different care settings, and building out additional AI capabilities to support clinical decision-making.

Bioliberty wants to be the technology provider that helps ensure that recovery does not stop when a patient leaves a rehabilitation facility. With a US base in Boston and partnerships with some of the most prominent rehabilitation providers in the United States, including a clinical study with Mount Sinai health system in 2024, it aims to become an end-to-end rehabilitation platform that works across hospital, post-acute, and home settings.

]]> Alethio Therapeutics (Alethio), an Abingdon-on-Thames-based biopharmaceutical company developing next-generation therapies for myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), has announced the completion of an oversubscribed €80.46 million ($90 million/£67 million) Series A financing.

The round was co-led by new investors Sofinnova Partners and RA Capital, alongside founding investor Oxford Science Enterprises, with additional support from Cancer Research Horizons and the University of Oxford. As part of the financing, Graziano Seghezzi, Managing Partner at Sofinnova Partners, and Maxwell DeNies of RA Capital have joined Alethio’s Board of Directors.

“The most transformative companies are built around insights that challenge long-held assumptions in medicine. In MPNs, the field has long accepted that controlling the disease is enough. Alethio challenges that assumption. By targeting the cells that drive the disease, its approach has the potential to move patients beyond symptom management toward true disease modification. All of this is based on an exceptional team and founders with a deep understanding of the disease,” said Graziano Seghezzi, Managing Partner at Sofinnova Partners.

Alethio was founded in 2021 as a spin-out from the University of Oxford by Professors Adam Mead and Beth Psaila, two globally recognised physician-scientists in MPNs. Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), including essential thrombocythaemia (ET), are blood cancers characterised by the uncontrolled production of blood cells and an increased risk of thrombosis, bone marrow scarring (myelofibrosis), and transformation to acute leukaemia, the UK startup explained. 

“Alethio Therapeutics was born from years of research at the University of Oxford and from our direct experience treating patients with MPNs. We founded the company to ensure that deep human disease insight and rigorous science translate into medicines that can alter disease progression, not just manage its symptoms. Our aim is to offer patients real hope — helping them live longer, healthier lives,” co-founders Mead and Psaila mentioned on the website. 

According to the company, current therapies for ET are non-targeted treatments that have been around for decades, such as hydroxycarbamide and interferon, that can affect, and disproportionately damage, healthy cells. 

Alethio claims to be pursuing a different approach, developing targeted therapies designed to selectively eliminate the disease-driving cells that sustain MPNs. The company notes that this approach modifies the underlying disease features, restores healthy blood counts, reduces thrombotic risk, and ultimately improves patient outcomes.

“Too often, a patient’s first encounter with ET is a thrombotic event that lands them in the emergency room. What follows is typically lifelong treatment with therapies that can cause burdensome side effects and are associated with high rates of resistance. Alethio was founded on a simple conviction – if you can selectively eliminate the cells driving disease, you can redefine what is possible for patients. This financing enables us to turn that conviction into reality,” said Dr. Rohit Batta, Chief Executive Officer of Alethio Therapeutics.

Alethio’s lead programme, ATX-011, is a first-in-class monoclonal antibody that targets G6B, designed to treat essential thrombocythaemia. G6B is a novel target in MPN, uniquely expressed on MPN-initiating stem cells but not on healthy stem cells. It is also expressed on megakaryocytes and platelets — the cells that drive thrombosis and transformation to myelofibrosis.

The UK startup highlighted that these findings support ATX-011’s potential to deliver broad therapeutic benefit across patients with MPNs, regardless of driver mutation. Alethio is advancing ATX-011 through IND-enabling studies and toward clinical development in ET.

It also reported that preclinical data for ATX-011 has been selected for oral presentation at the American Society of Hematology (ASH) 2026 Annual Meeting. 

The company has also built ARTEMIS (Advanced Research & Translational Engine for Myeloproliferative Neoplasms), which is an integrated discovery and development engine for MPNs. Alethio says ARTEMIS is designed to systematically identify, validate, and de-risk novel mutant drivers of disease and therapeutic candidates against these targets.

Powered by ARTEMIS, Alethio is building a pipeline of novel biologic disease-modifying therapies for MPNs. Alongside ATX-011, it is also developing a programme targeting mutant calreticulin (CALR)–driven disease, which occurs in roughly 30% of patients with MPNs.

“Since its formation, Alethio has made incredible progress in translating pioneering University of Oxford science into a focused and ambitious biotechnology company. The team has built not only a promising lead programme but also the ARTEMIS discovery platform, providing a powerful engine for future pipeline innovation. We are proud to continue supporting the company and are delighted to welcome such an experienced syndicate to help Alethio transition to the next stage of growth; delivering meaningful impact for patients in the clinic,” said Sally Dewhurst, Principal at Oxford Science Enterprises. 

The company plans to use this capital to transition into a clinical-stage company, deploying capital to advance its lead programme, ATX-011, through completion of Phase 1/2a studies in essential thrombocythaemia (ET) and to Phase 3 readiness, while also progressing additional MPN programmes toward IND submission.

]]> Vensum Power, a Helsinki-based developer of Software-Defined Power Conversion (SDPC) solution, has closed a €9 million Series A round.

The round was co-led by existing backer Lifeline Ventures alongside two new investors, Larsen & Toubro Group and Eviny Ventures. The round also saw continued participation from investors Grid.vc and Harjavalta Ventures. Vensum Power had raised €3.8 million Seed funding in 2023, and the Series A round brings its total funding to €15.2 million since its founding in 2018.

“Data centres are competing with every other sector for the same grid capacity, and Vensum Power tackles one of the most overlooked inefficiencies in the system: converting power into a form that equipment can use optimally,” said Prashant Chiranjive Jain, Managing Director of L&T Vyoma and Head of L&T Electronic Products & Systems, both business verticals of Larsen & Toubro.

He added, “The global energy transition and the growth of digital infrastructure both depend on getting this right, at scale. We are proud to support Vensum Power as it scales up across global markets and, in doing so, we help accelerate the energy transition.”

Vensum Power was founded in 2018 and currently employs around 20 people. It develops power conversion technology that it describes as near-lossless. While conventional power converters are engineered around a narrow peak-efficiency point and typically require redesign for each new application, Vensum’s product is designed to deliver high efficiency across fluctuating loads.

Vensum Power says its converters are among the world’s smallest at their power class, and engineered for use across AI data centres, EV charging stations, energy storage systems, renewable energy installations, and DC microgrids.

As electricity demand surges, driven by global electrification and AI infrastructure buildout, efficient power conversion has moved from a technical necessity to a foundational strategic need. Vensum Power is pitching its ability to deliver near-lossless power conversion as a critical advantage in environments like AI data centres, where workloads change rapidly, and every watt lost to heat must also be cooled.

The Finnish DeepTech company says it will use the fresh capital to scale its product from development to industrial-scale delivery. The company’s Software-Defined Power Conversion platform, which uses soft-switching techniques and digital control to minimise energy losses, is set to enter mass production at partner factories in 2027.

Initial products, Vensum Power says, will serve EV charging and energy storage markets, with AI data centres to follow as the next main target.

“The funding round propels us from developing technology to delivering it at industrial scale and bringing the same proven solution to AI data centres, where access to power has become the main bottleneck. The question in data centres is no longer only how powerful the chips are, but how efficiently the used electricity actually reaches them. Thanks to the software-defined approach, our converters operate consistently at extremely high efficiency even with rapidly changing loads,” said Peter Nisula, CEO of Vensum Power.

Near-lossless energy conversion has been one of the biggest challenges in the power sector; Vensum Power is advancing closer to that goal with its first products for EV charging and energy storage entering mass production. As Nisula noted, the critical question for AI data centres is not how powerful the chips are, but how efficiently the electricity actually reaches them, and if Vensum’s SDPC platform solves that at industrial scale, a problem the company is now moving to solve at scale.

]]> The European Commission has adopted the 2027 European Innovation Council (EIC) Work Programme, allocating €1.8 billion to support DeepTech startups, scale-ups and researchers across Europe.

The funding package aims to help promising technologies move from early-stage research to commercialisation, while improving access to investment for women-led and DefenceTech companies.

Ekaterina Zaharieva, Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, says: “This is how it puts our Startup and Scaleup Strategy into action: mobilising more capital, stimulating customer deals, cutting complexity, and making bold investments on the technologies that will shape our future. And, as we shape the next EU research and innovation programme, our task is to turn Europe’s scientific excellence, talent and industrial strength into new companies and lasting competitiveness.”

The programme marks the final EIC funding package under Horizon Europe 2021–2027, the EU’s research and innovation framework.

A significant part of the programme focuses on expanding access to growth capital. This includes completing the €1 billion commitment to the Scaleup Europe Fund, launched in 2026 and managed by investment firm EQT. The fund aims to attract at least €4 billion from other investors and support European technology companies through investments averaging more than €100 million.

Alongside this initiative, the EIC will continue supporting startups through its STEP Scale Up scheme, targeting companies developing strategic technologies. The 2027 programme also completes funding allocations of €200 million for defence investments and €25 million for the Advanced Innovation Challenges pilot, both introduced in 2026.

These measures form part of the EU Startup and Scaleup Strategy and the Competitiveness Compass, two initiatives intended to strengthen Europe’s innovation ecosystem and address obstacles faced by technology companies seeking to grow.

Established under Horizon Europe in 2021, the EIC has a budget exceeding €10 billion for the 2021–2027 period. Since its launch, it has supported more than 800 companies and nearly 700 research projects, providing financial assistance at different stages of technological development.

Its investment arm, the EIC Fund, has already invested close to €2 billion in more than 375 deep tech startups, attracting approximately 3.5 times that amount in co-investment.

The programme also expands support for women-led startups through a redesigned Women TechEU initiative, doubling individual grants to €150k. A new European Prize for Women Innovators in Quantum will also be introduced, complementing the existing European Prize for Women Innovators and recognising female entrepreneurs working in quantum technologies.

Another priority is helping EIC-backed startups secure their first customers. New measures will connect companies with public and private procurers, allowing them to test emerging technologies and explore potential commercial applications.

Support for dual-use and defence technologies will remain part of the EIC’s activities, reflecting the EU’s interest in strengthening its technological capabilities across strategic sectors.

At the same time, the Commission intends to reduce administrative complexity and make funding more accessible to innovators at different stages of development.

]]> Munich-based aviation startup VÆRIDION has raised €30 million in a Series A2 funding round and selected for a €94.5 million grant from the European Commission’s Innovation Fund, bringing the combined value to €124.5 million.

The investment round was co-led by Dutch investors SHIFT Invest and Invest-NL, with participation from existing backers World Fund, Project A and Vsquared Ventures. PAYBACK founder and DeepTech investor Alexander Rittweger also joined the round. VÆRIDION has raised approximately €60 million to date, excluding the newly announced EU grant.

Ivor van Dartel, founder and CEO of VÆRIDION, says: “Over the past year, we have turned the Microliner from a validated design into hardware, with exceptional capital efficiency. Our propulsion and battery technology is now being tested at our own facility in Oberpfaffenhofen. This equity round enables us to build our first conforming aircraft. The Commission’s selection of CAROLUS supports the next step: establishing the industrial capability for Microliner production.

“Building out of Europe, our mission is to make regional flying commercially viable and accessible again, in Europe and for operators worldwide.”

VÆRIDION’s announcement comes amid other European funding rounds for next-generation aircraft and aerospace technologies in 2026.

In France, AURA AERO announced a €50 million Series B to advance its electric and hybrid-electric aircraft programmes, while HyLight raised €13 million for hydrogen-powered autonomous airships. In the UK, Greenjets secured €35 million for aerospace propulsion technology and Skyfly raised €8.91 million for electric aircraft development.

Elsewhere, Denmark’s Acodyne secured €2.5 million for unmanned cargo aircraft, while Germany’s SPREAD AI raised €25 million for industrial engineering software serving sectors including aerospace.

Together with VÆRIDION’s €30 million equity round, these selected announcements represent approximately €164.4 million in financing, excluding VÆRIDION’s separately selected EU grant.

EU-Startups previously covered VÆRIDION’s €14 million Series A in December 2024, led by returning investor World Fund.

Daria Saharova, Managing Partner at World Fund, adds: “For the past half century, Airbus has shown that Europe can build aircraft the world buys. VÆRIDION is writing the next chapter with a fully electric aircraft, built in Bavaria, with a clear path to certification. Investing in the future of aviation is Europe’s power play, and I am proud to back Ivor and the team.”

Founded in 2021 by former Airbus manager Ivor van Dartel and headquartered in Munich, VÆRIDION is developing fully electric aircraft designed to make short-distance regional aviation more economically viable.

Its flagship aircraft, the Microliner, aims to carry nine passengers over distances of approximately 400 kilometres, connecting regional destinations that have become increasingly difficult to serve profitably using conventional aircraft.

The €30 million investment will finance the development of VÆRIDION’s first certification-conforming aircraft and further propulsion testing. Meanwhile, the €94.5 million Innovation Fund grant is intended to support the CAROLUS project, which will establish and scale up a final assembly facility at Oberpfaffenhofen Airport, near Munich.

The project was selected from 358 applications as one of 12 large-scale projects, making VÆRIDION the only German company and the only aviation project selected in this category. The grant remains subject to the completion of an agreement expected in 2027.

The Microliner combines a glider-inspired wing with patented modular battery technology and a multi-engine propulsion system driving a single propeller. It is being developed in passenger and cargo configurations, with a targeted range of 400 kilometres carrying nine passengers under Instrument Flight Rules, or up to 550 kilometres carrying four passengers under Visual Flight Rules.

The company is targeting operating costs below €0.40 per seat-kilometre, which it believes could allow operators to offer tickets at prices comparable to first-class journeys on Germany’s ICE high-speed trains. Its broader ambition is to restore regional connections, including services linking smaller German cities and airfields that are no longer served by commercial airlines.

Thijs Gitmans, General Partner at SHIFT Invest, adds: “Regional aviation is one of the clearest cases where electrification makes both environmental and commercial sense. VÆRIDION has chosen a certification pathway regulators already understand and has delivered real hardware on a disciplined budget. We are proud to lead this round and to back a European champion in electric flight with European funding.”

The company reports customer commitments for more than 130 aircraft, representing a potential value exceeding €730 million. Its launch customer is Belgium-based ASL Group, with the first Microliner delivery targeted for 2030.

In March 2026, VÆRIDION opened its production and testing facility at Oberpfaffenhofen Airport, where it has since powered on its electric engine for the first time. The facility was acquired following the insolvency of German electric aviation startup Lilium.

The startup is now preparing to integrate its battery packs and propulsion system into a ground-testing platform known as a copper bird. Alongside wind-tunnel testing, this work will support the development of its first certification-conforming prototype, currently targeted for late 2027 or early 2028.

With engineering activities in Munich and Delft, and production planned in Bavaria, VÆRIDION intends to expand its European team as it progresses towards flight testing, certification and industrial production.

The post Why did British Airways take over British Caledonian Airways in 1987? appeared first on AGN.

]]> The takeover of British Caledonian Airways by British Airways in 1987 was a defining moment in British aviation history. It brought together the UK’s largest airline and its most prominent independent rival, reshaping competition and the future of commercial air travel in Britain.

The deal was driven by several factors, including British Caledonian’s financial difficulties, British Airways’ ambitions to compete internationally, concerns about foreign ownership and the potential benefits of combining the two airlines.

However, the proposed takeover also raised significant concerns about competition and the dominance of British Airways in the UK aviation market. Understanding why the takeover happened requires looking at the history of both airlines and the economic and political circumstances of the 1980s.

Who was British Caledonian Airways?

British Caledonian, commonly known as BCal, was established in 1970 when Caledonian Airways acquired British United Airways. It began operating under the British Caledonian name in 1971, becoming an important independent competitor to the UK’s established airline businesses.

Based at London Gatwick Airport, BCal operated scheduled and charter flights to destinations across Europe, Africa, North America and elsewhere. Its distinctive branding, featuring the Scottish lion rampant, helped establish a strong identity.

BCal was also significant because it represented the government’s ambition to create a stronger independent airline capable of challenging the established national carriers. It developed an international network and became a recognised alternative to British Airways.

However, despite its achievements, BCal faced considerable financial and operational challenges during the 1980s. These difficulties eventually made the airline vulnerable to a takeover.

British Caledonian was experiencing financial difficulties

One of the main reasons British Airways took over BCal was the smaller airline’s weakening financial position.

Operating an international airline required substantial investment in aircraft, staff, maintenance, airport facilities and route development. BCal also faced intense competition in an industry affected by economic uncertainty and changing passenger demand.

Although the airline had established an extensive route network, it lacked the financial resources and scale available to some of its larger competitors.

A government-backed route exchange in 1984 was intended to strengthen BCal by giving it access to additional international opportunities. However, the Saudi Arabian routes it received subsequently declined in importance, limiting the anticipated financial benefits.

By 1987, BCal was exploring alternative arrangements to secure its future. These included discussions with Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) about potential investment and operational cooperation.

British Airways recognised that BCal’s financial vulnerability created an opportunity to acquire a significant competitor and expand its own operations.

British Airways wanted to strengthen its international position

British Airways had its own reasons for pursuing the takeover. Following its privatisation in February 1987, the airline was seeking to strengthen its commercial position and compete more effectively against major international airlines.

The global aviation market was becoming increasingly competitive. Airlines needed extensive networks, substantial investment and sufficient financial resources to operate successfully across international markets.

Acquiring BCal offered British Airways an opportunity to expand its operations by incorporating aircraft, routes, staff and other business assets. The takeover could also create operational efficiencies by combining certain activities and reducing duplicated costs.

In July 1987, British Airways announced its intention to purchase BCal for approximately £237 million. The agreement was presented as a way to strengthen the British airline industry’s international competitiveness while protecting BCal from potential financial collapse.

The deal therefore offered British Airways both commercial advantages and a means of consolidating its position in the global aviation market.

The threat of foreign ownership

Another important factor was the possibility that BCal might be acquired by a foreign airline or investor. BCal was considering a potential arrangement with SAS, while other interested parties were also exploring opportunities involving the airline.

British Airways argued that a takeover by another organisation could threaten BCal’s position as a British international carrier, particularly because airline route licences were subject to regulatory requirements.

The prospect of foreign ownership helped strengthen the case for a deal that would keep BCal under British control. However, this argument was also commercially convenient for British Airways. Acquiring BCal would prevent a rival investor from obtaining its aircraft, routes and other valuable assets.

The takeover was therefore about more than rescuing a struggling airline. It was also a strategic decision about who would control an important part of Britain’s aviation industry.

Combining routes, aircraft and operations

BCal had an established international route network and a significant presence at Gatwick. Acquiring the airline offered British Airways the opportunity to expand its operations and incorporate valuable business assets.

The two airlines also operated in overlapping markets, meaning that combining their businesses could generate cost savings. Potential benefits included consolidating certain administrative functions, coordinating aircraft and maintenance resources, and integrating commercial operations.

However, the takeover was not simply a matter of combining two businesses without complications. Their existing routes overlapped, and the merger raised questions about how much competition would remain after the acquisition.

British Airways also needed to address regulatory requirements concerning route licences and airport access.

Although the acquisition strengthened BA’s position, some of BCal’s routes and operations were subsequently transferred, surrendered or reorganised as part of the merger process.

Why was the takeover controversial?

Despite its potential commercial benefits, the proposed takeover attracted significant criticism. BCal had been an important independent competitor, and its absorption into British Airways threatened to reduce consumer choice and increase the dominance of the country’s largest airline.

The UK government referred the proposed merger to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) for investigation.

In November 1987, the commission identified potential benefits, including improved international competitiveness, financial savings and a reduced risk of BCal’s failure.

However, it also highlighted concerns about reduced competition, British Airways’ market power and possible disadvantages for other airlines operating from Gatwick.

There were additional concerns that British Airways might restrict competitors’ access to maintenance and training facilities previously provided by BCal.

To address these issues, BA agreed to significant concessions. These included surrendering at least 5,000 landing slots at Gatwick and returning various route licences, creating opportunities for competing airlines to operate services.

The conditions demonstrated that the government recognised the potential benefits of the takeover but wanted to limit its impact on competition.

When was the takeover completed?

British Airways announced the proposed acquisition on 16 July 1987. The transaction subsequently underwent regulatory scrutiny before receiving approval subject to conditions.

BA secured majority control of BCal’s parent company in December 1987, and the merger was completed in 1988. The acquisition marked the end of BCal as a major independent scheduled airline.

Its aircraft, employees, routes and other operations were incorporated into British Airways, although some activities were reorganised following the merger.

BCal’s distinctive identity did not disappear entirely. British Airways later revived the Caledonian name for its charter operations, preserving elements of the brand’s heritage.

What was the impact of the takeover?

The takeover strengthened British Airways by expanding its assets and consolidating its position in the UK aviation market. It also demonstrated the challenges facing smaller independent airlines competing against larger international carriers with greater financial resources and broader networks.

For passengers, the merger had mixed implications. A stronger airline could benefit from greater operational resources and a wider network, but reduced competition raised concerns about fares, choice and service quality.

The regulatory concessions were intended to protect competing airlines and preserve opportunities for other operators, particularly at Gatwick.

The takeover also marked a turning point in British aviation policy. The government’s earlier ambition to establish a strong independent competitor to the national airline effectively came to an end when BCal was absorbed into British Airways.

British Airways strengthened its international presence

British Airways took over British Caledonian because the deal offered a combination of commercial, financial and strategic advantages.

BCal was experiencing financial difficulties and faced an uncertain future, while British Airways wanted to strengthen its international position following privatisation. The potential for foreign ownership, opportunities to combine operations and the value of BCal’s route network also influenced the decision.

However, the acquisition was controversial because it reduced competition in the British aviation market. Regulatory approval came with conditions designed to protect rival airlines and preserve opportunities for competition.

Ultimately, the takeover reshaped the UK airline industry. It strengthened British Airways, ended BCal’s independence and illustrated the difficult balance between building internationally competitive airlines and maintaining a competitive domestic market.

]]> Sam Bousfield, Founder and CEO of Samson Sky, says Tesla’s flying Roadster demonstration has renewed public interest in flying cars. However, manufacturers still face significant challenges involving certification, insurance and practical design.

Elon Musk’s demonstration of a hovering Tesla Roadster could help bring flying cars closer to commercial reality by renewing public interest in the technology, Bousfield said.

Speaking exclusively to Aerospace Global News, Bousfield described Tesla’s demonstration as good news for an industry that has spent decades trying to turn flying cars into a commercially viable form of transport.

“I think that it was great that he did what he did. He makes the impossible possible,” Bousfield said. “I think that reignited the interest in flying cars, and I think that’s a good thing for the overall industry.”

His company has spent 18 years developing the Switchblade, a three-wheeled roadable aircraft with retractable wings and a folding tail. Unlike Tesla’s hovering concept, the Switchblade is designed to drive on public roads and take off from conventional airports.

Samson Sky is now targeting production within 18 months, following a redesign to improve the aircraft’s performance.

Why has it taken so long to develop a commercially viable flying car?

Although flying cars have existed in various experimental forms since the 1950s, manufacturers have struggled to develop vehicles that are practical enough for regular use. Bousfield believes the problem starts with the design.

“It’s difficult to make something that is of high enough performance that people will want to have and still make it do what you want it to do both in driving and flying,” he explained.

For Samson Sky, the answer was to design a vehicle around the requirements of both modes of transport rather than modifying an existing car to fly.

“We asked the question, what’s the best layout for a driving and flying vehicle? Most people asked the question, ‘how do you make a car fly?’ And that difference in question gave a different answer.”

The Switchblade’s wings and tail fold away into its body for road use. At an airport, they deploy to convert the vehicle into a fixed-wing aircraft.

Bousfield said the objective was to make a vehicle owners could use frequently rather than something intended primarily for demonstrations.

“The main difference that we found in our approach is to try to make it a practical flying car from the get-go, from the beginning, and something that people could use often. Not maybe a daily driver, but often.”

Performance has been particularly challenging. Bousfield said customers willing to pay for a flying car would expect it to be competitive with conventional transport.

“They don’t pay big money to have something slow,” he said.

How Samson Sky is navigating aviation and road regulations

Bousfield considers regulation one of the greatest barriers to commercialising flying cars.

In the United States, manufacturers must meet the Federal Aviation Administration‘s aircraft requirements while also meeting road vehicle regulations administered by federal and state authorities.

“And those two sets of rules don’t mesh. They don’t talk,” he said. “It’s a really tough go to use those two sets of rules, ground and air, and make a go of it. And that’s, I think, the biggest problem that has kept a commercially successful flying car from happening.”

Samson Sky has approached this problem by choosing regulatory classifications that allow greater design flexibility.

For flight, the Switchblade is being developed under the FAA’s Experimental Amateur-Built aircraft category rather than conventional aircraft type certification.

“On the ground, we were lucky as our three-wheel solution is seen as a motorcycle in the US and many countries, and the regulations for motorcycles are fairly small and easily met,” Bousfield said. “We still have two masters (air and ground), but their rules are easy enough to meet that we can be successful as a business.”

Samson’s build-your-own flying car

The experimental amateur-built classification requires amateurs to undertake most of the aircraft’s fabrication and assembly for their own education or recreation.

Samson Sky intends to meet this requirement through a manufacturing process in which customers operate computer-controlled equipment to produce parts for their aircraft.

Bousfield explained that customers would learn to operate six machines and produce components under controlled conditions.

“In our case, we use the making of the parts as the 50% or 51% because it’s easier and it’s more controlled,” he said.

He said the FAA had accepted the company’s proposed approach, which would allow trained Samson Sky personnel to complete final assembly through a 33-step production process with quality-control checks.

The experimental category does not remove the requirement for an individual aircraft to obtain the appropriate airworthiness approval or for its pilot to hold the necessary qualifications.

Why insurance could be another obstacle for flying cars

Certification is not the only concern for prospective flying car owners. Bousfield also believes manufacturers must address the practical question of insurance.

“Insurance is a big concern of pilots. Drivers take insurance for granted, as it is easy to get. Insurance for aircraft is often not as easily obtained,” he said. “For flying cars, there will need to be two insurance policies to begin with: one for flight and one for driving.”

Bousfield expects obtaining road insurance for the Switchblade to be relatively straightforward.

“The driving for us would be fairly easy, as there are many insurance brokers who provide insurance for kit cars, which we would be classed as for insurance purposes on the ground,” he said.

Flight insurance presents a different challenge. “Insurers for flight have told us many times over the years that they will only insure a flying car that fully protects the wings, tail and propellers while on the ground,” he said. “The Switchblade was designed with that in mind, and we are the only vehicle to fully protect flight surfaces while driving.”

Flying cars could serve a different market from eVTOL air taxis

Bousfield does not see conventional flying cars competing directly with electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft being developed for urban air taxi services. He believes the two technologies will serve different journey lengths and operating requirements.

“The VTOL is really good at one thing, which is short distance and rapid turnaround,” he said. “It can get you from this rooftop to this rooftop or from the airport to the city, and, you know, under 50 miles, that works.”

The Switchblade is intended for longer regional journeys. “We go between centres. We go between urban centres and are the regional approach.”

Bousfield believes the United States’ extensive general aviation airport network makes this model particularly attractive. He pointed out that the country has thousands of public-use airports, relatively few of which have scheduled commercial airline services. 

“In the United States, for instance, there are 5,000 public-use airports in the country. There are only 330 that have commercial service,” he said. “And so with the Switchblade, you can utilise not only the 5,000 public airports, but the 8,000 private airports, if they’ll allow you to land or take off from there, and greatly expand the places that you can get to.”

This network could let Switchblade owners fly closer to their destinations than scheduled airline services allow, then complete the final part of their journey by road.

Samson Sky is targeting regional journeys of approximately 200 to 500 miles (320 to 800km), with a flying speed of around 160mph (257km/h). 

Who would buy a flying car?

Bousfield believes the first customers will primarily be people who want greater flexibility for business and leisure travel.

“Our customers have told us that their biggest use is both personal and pleasure,” he said.

He gave the example of someone operating several businesses in different locations who could fly between them without relying on airline schedules or spending long periods driving.

“So, it allows him to travel on his terms, wherever he wants, whenever he wants, and be like a personal airline for him.”

Bousfield also sees a potential corporate market for the Switchblade, particularly among businesses employing specialist staff who regularly travel between distant work sites. He suggested that a roadable aircraft could allow employees to fly to a regional airport, drive between nearby appointments and return home the same evening.

“And then they fly home for dinner,” he said. “I think that’s going to be a really key thing for businesses to benefit from and retain their key staff and their ability to provide the service that they need.”

Could the Switchblade eventually become electric?

Although the Switchblade’s current propulsion approach uses automotive gasoline, Bousfield said the aircraft was originally conceived with hybrid-electric technology in mind.

“It was originally conceived to be at least a hybrid-electric. That’s what my first design was,” he said. “We went with gasoline to start with and then are circling back now to hybrid because it’s now making sense, and we figured out how we can do it.”

Bousfield said the company chose gasoline because burning leaded aviation fuel in residential neighbourhoods would be unacceptable, making automotive fuel a more practical solution. He acknowledged that battery weight remains a significant obstacle to fully electric regional aircraft.

“The batteries are basically dead weight for us at this point,” he said. “But being hybrid electric, we’re setting ourselves up to be able to convert to full electric in the future, which is ideal as soon as battery technology allows us to do that.”

Switchblade production target follows 18 years of development

Samson Sky’s route towards production has not been straightforward. The company flew an earlier Switchblade prototype but discovered that it did not meet its intended maximum speed.

Bousfield said the setback came as the company prepared to enter production about three years ago.

“We met everything else, all our performance requirements for the ground. It flew well, but we didn’t hit our top speed with that design,” he said. “We promised high performance. People are expecting that, and we have to give it to them.”

Samson Sky returned to the drawing board, undertaking further design and wind tunnel work to address the shortfall.

Bousfield said the experience was a difficult lesson after years of development.

“Even when you think you’re done, sometimes it doesn’t work 100%.” He credits the company’s investors and supporters with helping sustain the programme through its lengthy development.

“If it were just me, I would have given up, but I had investors. I had people counting on it and people who looked at us and liked the product, and I just didn’t want to give up on that dream of people and my own dream.”

How soon will flying cars be common?

The company is now targeting an assembly line and the start of production within approximately 18 months.

Bousfield also identified PAL-V and Slovakia’s Klein Vision among the manufacturers working to bring flying cars into production. He does not expect flying cars to become as commonplace as conventional automobiles immediately. Instead, he believes they will gradually enter everyday use and gain wider acceptance.

“It’s like the first electric cars when they came out. It’s like, oh, there’s one, and then you wait another day and a half. Oh, there’s one,” he said. “So it takes seeing them and knowing that they’re real for it to be something that really takes hold of the imagination of most people.”

Tesla’s hovering Roadster demonstration may have helped revive public interest in flying cars. Still, Bousfield’s experience suggests that getting these vehicles into regular use will depend on solving the less visible problems of manufacturing, regulation, insurance and practical operation.

]]> What is clear-air turbulence and why is it so dangerous for pilots? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/dangers-invisible-turbulence-pilots Sun, 08 Nov 2026 10:17:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55527 Clear-air turbulence is an increasing threat to aviation safety, leaving flight crews facing unexpected challenges at cruising altitude.

The post What is clear-air turbulence and why is it so dangerous for pilots? appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • Clear-air turbulence is invisible to weather radar, making sudden, hard-to-predict encounters a persistent risk at cruising altitude.
  • Climate change is intensifying turbulence; severe North Atlantic clear-air turbulence increased 55% between 1979 and 2020.
  • Aircraft withstand turbulence, but unrestrained passengers and crew face serious injury risks from sudden violent movements.

Clear-air turbulence is a growing concern for the aviation industry, with changing weather patterns potentially making encounters more frequent and severe.

Unlike storm-related turbulence, it can strike without warning, even when the sky appears completely clear.

What is clear-air turbulence?

Clear-air turbulence (CAT) is turbulence that occurs in cloudless skies and cannot be detected by conventional onboard weather radar.

Typically found at cruising altitude, clear-air turbulence (CAT) is closely linked to jet streams and sudden changes in wind speed and direction. These variations, known as wind shear, can disrupt airflow around an aircraft, causing sudden and sometimes violent movements.

Can pilots detect clear-air turbulence?

Weather radar is an essential tool, helping crews identify precipitation and steer clear of thunderstorms. However, it cannot directly detect clear-air turbulence, leaving flight crews reliant on other sources of information.

Weather forecasts, reports from nearby aircraft and updates from air traffic control all help pilots assess conditions along their route. However, the information is not always timely or accurate enough to prevent an encounter.

Atmospheric conditions can change quickly, meaning a report from another aircraft may no longer reflect what is happening when the next flight passes through. This makes it harder for pilots to plan their routes and avoid affected areas.

See also: How much extra fuel does an airliner need to carry in case something goes wrong? See also: How much extra fuel does an airliner need to carry in case something goes wrong?

How is climate change increasing the risk of severe turbulence?

Research from the University of Reading suggests climate change is contributing to an increase in clear-air turbulence. A 2023 study examining atmospheric conditions between 1979 and 2020 found that, over an average point in the North Atlantic, the annual duration of severe turbulence increased by 55%. Moderate and light turbulence also rose by 37% and 17% respectively.


These changes are associated with shifts in atmospheric temperatures and wind patterns. As the planet warms, differences in temperature between regions can affect jet stream strength and behaviour, potentially creating greater wind shear.

This has particular implications for long-haul operators, whose aircraft regularly fly through major jet stream corridors. Understanding how these patterns are changing will be important when planning routes and assessing potential hazards.

How dangerous is clear-air turbulence?

Although commercial aircraft are designed to withstand considerable aerodynamic forces, passengers and cabin crew are more exposed to injury during sudden movements. Anyone not wearing a seatbelt can be thrown from their seat, potentially suffering serious injuries.

These dangers were highlighted by Singapore Airlines flight SQ321 in May 2024. The Boeing 777 encountered severe turbulence while travelling from London to Singapore, resulting in one passenger fatality and numerous injuries.

For pilots, incidents like this show the importance of cabin safety alongside aircraft handling. Crews may suspend meal services, ask passengers to return to their seats and request a different flight level when needed.

Also read: Why are airlines keeping older aircraft in service for longer? Also read: Why are airlines keeping older aircraft in service for longer?

How do airlines predict turbulence?

Better information could help pilots make more informed decisions before reaching areas of unstable air. IATA’s Turbulence Aware platform is one example, sharing turbulence reports from participating aircraft with other operators. This gives flight crews and airline operations teams a broader picture of conditions along their routes.

Researchers are also exploring lidar technology, which uses laser pulses to detect changes in atmospheric density ahead of an aircraft. Although it is not yet a standard solution for commercial fleets, it could eventually provide pilots with an extra way of identifying hazardous conditions.

For the time being, improved forecasting, aircraft-to-aircraft data sharing and established cockpit procedures are central to managing the risk.

What does the future hold for turbulence and flight safety?

By its nature, clear-air turbulence is difficult to predict and there will always be situations where pilots have little opportunity to avoid it. However, better access to atmospheric data and advances in detection technology could give crews more time to respond.

As the aviation industry adapts to changing atmospheric conditions, improving its ability to forecast and manage clear-air turbulence will remain an important part of protecting passengers and crews.

]]> The three big European legacy airline groups released their third quarter (Q3) results over the last two weeks, demonstrating how they performed during the all-important summer period where they generate most of the year’s revenue.

The International Airlines Group (IAG), Lufthansa Group and Air France-KLM all suffered from higher fuel prices. For all three, the fuel bill increased by about 30% in Q3 2026 compared to last year.

While hedging helped cushion the blow, it did not fully mitigate the surge. By contrast, U.S. carriers -which largely eschew fuel hedging – saw their fuel bills skyrocket by as much as 69%.

Revenue increases helped mitigate part of the increase in fuel costs

Lufthansa Group continued to lag behind Air France-KLM and International Airlines Group.

Fuel took on a larger share of Lufthansa’s overall expenses, reaching roughly 22%. This remains lower than its peers, with fuel accounting for approximately 30% of expenses at IAG and 25% at Air France-KLM.

That said, Lufthansa’s costs are significantly higher than the other two in absolute terms, driven by substantial non-fuel costs from its Lufthansa Technik subsidiary. However, the subsidiary generates considerable revenue, up 20% year-on-year.

Lufthansa led the trio in total revenue growth, rising 9% to just over €12.2 billion. Air France-KLM followed with €9.9 billion (up 8%), while IAG recorded €9.7 billion, a modest 5% increase.

Low-cost subsidiaries performed best across all three airline groups

Looking at individual airlines, low-cost units outperformed their premium peers across all three airline groups.

For IAG, Vueling led the way with a healthy 23.8% operating margin this quarter. Lufthansa’s point-to-point business segment generated an 18.7% margin. This mainly comprises Eurowings, but also considers Eurowings Holidays and the equity investment in joint-venture SunExpress. Finally, for Air France-KLM, the low-cost Transavia branch held a 16.3% operating margin, considerably higher than the Paris-based unit at 13.5% and KLM at 11.4%.

Iberia’s performance was particularly noteworthy considering its high margins, as well as Aer Lingus and Austrian. Lufthansa Airlines remained at the bottom of the list with a 6% margin. The airline’s primary value stems from its intercontinental business, CEO Carsten Spohr reiterated in the group’s third-quarter earnings call.

Vueling and KLM had the highest load factors during the quarter, with 91.9% and 89.9% respectively.

International Airlines Group focuses on protecting profitability and growing premium capacity

IAG boasted the highest margins amongst Europe’s major airline groups at 17.7%. Despite a reduction of over 4 percentage points, its performance was robust. Healthy demand and solid revenue performance helped mitigate some of the impact of higher fuel prices. It saw strong yields across all markets.

The group’s executives pointed to ongoing disruption in the Middle East, air traffic control-induced flight disruption and higher fuel costs as concerns this quarter. British Airways was particularly affected by flight disruption and also Heathrow baggage system failures, group CFO José Antonio Barrionuevo said in the earnings call.

Capacity at Vueling and Iberia was reduced to “protect profitability” in what is a competitive short-haul environment, which helped drive unit revenue in the European market.

Meanwhile, overall corporate travel performance is “strong” driven by technology and the banking sectors that are “doing better,” IAG CEO Luis Gallego said. British Airways CEO Sean Doyle also said that this performance was also driven by “really strong demand from smaller businesses” trading in and out of the UK. Transit corporate demand from the US and India also helped results this quarter.

The group continues to focus on its premiumisation strategy. Recently, it announced that it would reconfigure its Airbus A380 fleet with the world’s largest business class cabin featuring 106 Club Suites.

Air France-KLM to restructure its Amsterdam portfolio

Though KLM’s operating margin improved, the group announced that the Amsterdam-based subsidiary would be undergoing a restructure to ensure its future cost efficiency. In light of the recent decree limiting the number of flights at Amsterdam Schiphol Airport, CEO Benjamin Smith noted that changes now needed to be made to “further establish a stronger financial foundation for a sustainable KLM.”

While its operating margin reached 11.4% for the quarter, year-to-date performance has not been as strong. It achieved a 4.8% margin for the first nine months of 2026, showing that its ‘Back on Track’ program has not been sufficient to achieve the Group target of an operating margin above 8%. It will decrease the number of positions at KLM by about 5,000 in total. It will also use Embraer E195-E2s to replace planned A320 fleet growth in the future, ensuring a smaller European feeder operation for its core long-haul network.

Smith clarified that previously KLM was a “real volume market” focusing on low-cost connections. However, with rising costs imposed by the Dutch government, it now has to focus on feeding more profitable long-haul connections and streamline capacity accordingly. It will also work to focus on capturing a “greater share of the local market” in Amsterdam which may provide yield uplift.

This forms part of its premium strategy as it sees revenue growth in non-economy cabins. Smith noted an “upmarket shift” across the group, with the share of revenues generated by business and Air France’s La Première increasing from 26% to 29%. Premium Economy’s share rose one percentage point to 8%. Overall, premium revenues now account for 37% of its total, up four points compared to 2024.  

Luthansa Group studying future of its Vienna and Brussels portfolios

In its earnings call, the German-headquartered group recognised that its network airlines segment remains in a fragile position and pointed to the underperformance of the flagship Lufthansa Airlines unit. Its other airlines, namely Austrian, SWISS and Brussels Airlines saw result improvements during the period.

CFO Till Streichert admitted that at Lufthansa Airlines “limited capacity growth and additional strike-related customer compensation payments weighed on the result.”

He described the turnaround program as “a key lever for further earnings improvement” moving forward. He pointed to strict cost discipline but also improvements to widebody utilisation and productivity as it reduces the “share of widebody reserve aircraft by about a fourth.”

Another highlight included healthy improvements in ancillary revenues for its network airlines, helping drive a growth in revenue.

“The good performance was primarily driven by strong yields, but also by very strong ancillary revenues, which increased by 21% versus last year,” Spohr shared. “This growth was supported on the one hand by an enhanced fare structure, but also by upgrades at an unseen level, and by the more differentiated offerings of our new onboard products, Allegris and SWISS Senses.

Moving forward, Spohr also suggested that the group was looking at optimising its Austrian Airlines and Brussels Airlines units. While admitting that they are “profitable operations” that “do create value,” he revealed that the group is studying whether an AOC is needed at every hub or whether they can be merged.

“We believe there could be less local value creation in terms of admin, in terms of things which can be done jointly,” he added.

Aviation experts explain what happens https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/can-planes-fall-out-sky Sat, 07 Nov 2026 15:57:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55522 Aircraft are engineered to withstand extraordinary forces, but the physics of flight leave little room for error. Here we examine the mechanics behind aerodynamic stalls, severe icing, loss of control and structural failure, exploring the factors that can turn a routine flight into a battle to stay airborne.

The post Can planes really fall out of the sky? Aviation experts explain what happens appeared first on AGN.

]]> The idea of an aircraft suddenly dropping out of the sky is frankly terrifying. Yet while it makes for a dramatic headline, the reality is considerably more complicated – and thankfully exceptionally unusual.

Aircraft are designed with multiple layers of protection against losing control, but under certain circumstances, a combination of aerodynamic forces, weather and mechanical problems can overwhelm even the most sophisticated aircraft.

The tragic Learjet 60 crash in Florida recently is a sobering reminder of how quickly things can go wrong. The aircraft, which was travelling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, crashed in Palm Beach County on Sunday, killing all nine people aboard.

In communications with air traffic control shortly before the accident, the crew reported icing, moderate turbulence and deteriorating weather conditions, followed by an extremely rapid descent.

According to preliminary statements from NTSB investigators, there is evidence the aircraft may have begun breaking up before impact, although the circumstances remain under investigation

It is too early to draw conclusions about what happened. However, the circumstances raise a wider question around what actually causes an aircraft to lose altitude so dramatically.

What causes an aircraft to come down?

Among the many reasons an aircraft can lose altitude rapidly is an aerodynamic stall. Investigators have not indicated whether a stall played any role in the Florida accident, but the event has prompted renewed interest in how stalls occur and why they can be dangerous.

Despite the popular association with engine failure, a stall has nothing directly to do with an engine stopping.

It occurs when the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack, causing airflow to separate from the wing surface and lift to reduce sharply. The aircraft may pitch down, roll or enter an uncontrolled descent.

Stalls can happen at almost any speed if the angle of attack becomes high enough.

Ice makes this even more dangerous. Even a relatively small accumulation on a wing can disrupt the airflow, reducing lift while increasing drag. It can also change the aircraft’s stall characteristics, sometimes leaving pilots with less warning than they would normally expect.

Serving airline Captain and aviation safety specialist Pete Wilson told us:

“An aircraft can fall out of the sky for numerous reasons. It could be structural failure, such as part of the airframe breaking away, a control surface malfunction, for example a rudder failure, or a problem with the trim system. It could also be a loss of control caused by aerodynamic conditions such as ice, thunderstorms, severe turbulence or wind shear.”

He added:

“Another possibility is cargo shifting during flight. A good example is the Boeing 747 crash at Bagram, Afghanistan, in 2013, when an unsecured military vehicle shifted towards the rear of the aircraft shortly after take-off, damaging critical systems and leaving the pilots unable to control the aircraft. Not every failure is engine-related.”

Can an aircraft break apart during a rapid descent?

An aircraft descending rapidly can accelerate beyond its operating limits, known as overspeed condition. The resulting aerodynamic loads can become severe, potentially exceeding the structural limits of the airframe. In extreme circumstances, components or entire sections of the aircraft can separate.

Importantly, a steep descent does not necessarily mean an aircraft has suffered a structural failure. A jet can lose thousands of feet per minute while remaining largely intact.

Equally, what looks like an aircraft falling straight down may actually be the final result of it losing control earlier in the flight.

Florida Learjet crash: NTSB probes evidence aircraft broke up before impact Florida Learjet crash: NTSB probes evidence aircraft broke up before impact

Why engine failure does not necessarily mean a crash

An engine failure on its own is unlikely to make an aircraft suddenly lose height and crash. Most multi-engine aircraft can remain controllable following the loss of an engine, while even a complete loss of thrust does not mean an aircraft immediately stops flying.

Aircraft can glide, sometimes over considerable distances, depending on altitude, speed and configuration.

Aircraft accidents are rarely down to a single failure

It’s extremely rare for an aircraft to go from flying normally to falling out of control in an instant. Usually, a series of things goes wrong, sometimes within seconds, until the pilots can no longer keep the aircraft stabilised.

This is why accident investigations are so important. Investigators need to work out not just what happened at the end, but what led up to it, how different problems may have affected the aircraft and why safety systems were unable to prevent the crash.

]]> Why airlines abandoned the upper deck lounge era https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/why-airlines-abandoned-upper-deck-lounges/ Sat, 07 Nov 2026 11:49:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55546 There was a time when using the upper deck spaces on Boeing 747s for lounges and cocktail bars became the norm for long-haul premium travellers.

The post Why airlines abandoned the upper deck lounge era appeared first on AGN.

]]> For a brief period in aviation history, flying was about more than simply getting from one destination to another. On some of the world’s most luxurious aircraft, passengers could leave their seats, head upstairs and enjoy a drink in an exclusive lounge thousands of feet above the ground.

The upper-deck lounge became one of the most memorable features of the golden age of commercial aviation. From elegant cocktail bars to spacious social areas, these spaces represented an era when airlines competed to make the journey itself an experience.

Yet today, such lounges are almost entirely a thing of the past. So what happened to this distinctive feature of air travel?

The golden age of onboard lounges

The introduction of large, wide-bodied aircraft during the late 1960s transformed commercial aviation. Among the most important was the Boeing 747, which entered airline service in 1970.

Its distinctive hump-backed design created an opportunity that airlines were quick to exploit. The upper deck, initially relatively small, could be transformed into an exclusive passenger space.

Airlines including Pan Am, American Airlines and other international carriers experimented with upstairs lounges, cocktail bars and social areas. Some featured comfortable armchairs, tables, elegant lighting and even piano-style entertainment.

For premium passengers, these spaces offered something that conventional aircraft cabins could not: the freedom to get up, socialise and enjoy a drink away from their seats. The upper deck became a powerful marketing tool, helping airlines distinguish themselves in an increasingly competitive international travel market.

The Boeing 747 made it possible

Although the 747 was primarily designed to carry large numbers of passengers, its unusual upper-deck configuration gave airlines considerable flexibility.

Early versions featured a relatively short upper deck, leaving room for a staircase connecting the main cabin to the lounge above. The space was particularly attractive to first-class passengers, who could enjoy a more exclusive environment during long-haul flights.

However, not every airline used the area in the same way. Some installed dedicated bars, while others opted for smaller lounges or additional seating.

As the 747 evolved, the upper deck was gradually extended on later versions (-300, -400, -8I), allowing airlines to accommodate more passengers in business and first class. This marked the beginning of the end for the traditional upstairs lounge.

Economics began to outweigh luxury

One of the biggest reasons airlines abandoned onboard lounges was financial. Every square metre of an aircraft cabin represents potential revenue. A lounge containing comfortable seating, a bar and social space could accommodate far fewer paying passengers than a conventional seating arrangement.

As airlines became increasingly focused on profitability, dedicating valuable cabin space to passengers who might only use it occasionally became difficult to justify. The economics became even more challenging as premium cabins evolved.

Airlines discovered that passengers were often willing to pay considerably more for private suites, fully flat beds and enhanced personal service.

Rather than providing a shared social space, carriers could generate additional revenue by installing more premium seats. The lounge was increasingly viewed as an expensive luxury rather than a profitable investment.

Changing passenger expectations

Passenger expectations also changed significantly. During the early decades of commercial jet travel, flying was often considered a special occasion. Passengers dressed formally, enjoyed elaborate meals and appreciated the opportunity to socialise during long journeys.

Modern air travel is considerably different nowadays. Business travellers increasingly prioritise privacy, comfort and the ability to work during flights. Leisure passengers, meanwhile, often value entertainment systems, personal space and comfortable seating.

The introduction of individual entertainment screens, improved connectivity and increasingly sophisticated premium cabins reduced the appeal of communal lounges. Today’s business-class passenger may prefer a private suite with a lie-flat bed over a shared cocktail bar.

Safety and operational considerations

Safety and operational requirements also played a role. Aircraft interiors must comply with strict regulations covering emergency evacuation, passenger movement, and cabin safety.

Dedicated lounges add challenges, especially when passengers move during turbulence or the aircraft encounters unexpected conditions. Open social spaces also require careful consideration of passenger circulation and crew responsibilities.

Although lounges were not inherently unsafe, their operational demands added another layer of complexity for airlines already seeking to simplify cabin layouts.

The rise of airport lounges

Another important development was the growing popularity of premium airport lounges. Airlines increasingly invested in luxurious ground facilities where passengers could enjoy restaurant-quality food, comfortable seating, showers, bars and business facilities before boarding. These lounges offered several advantages over their airborne counterparts.

They were larger, easier to maintain and could accommodate passengers from multiple flights. They also allowed airlines to provide a premium experience without sacrificing valuable aircraft cabin space.

For many travellers, the airport lounge became the place to relax and socialise, while the aircraft itself became a more functional environment focused on reaching the destination comfortably.

Could upper-deck lounges ever return?

Although traditional upper-deck cocktail bars have largely disappeared, the idea of creating distinctive social spaces onboard aircraft has never completely vanished. Some modern airlines (such as Virgin Atlantic) have introduced onboard bars and dedicated social areas, particularly on long-haul aircraft such as the Airbus A380.

Emirates, for example, is well known for its first-class and business-class onboard lounge and bar on the A380, while other carriers have experimented with communal spaces and premium cabin features.

These modern interpretations demonstrate that passengers still appreciate the opportunity to move around and socialise during long flights. However, they are generally more compact and carefully integrated into the cabin design than the elaborate lounges of aviation’s earlier decades.

An aviation luxury that belongs to another era

The disappearance of the upper-deck lounge reflects a much wider transformation in commercial aviation.

Airlines have moved away from the idea that luxury necessarily means grand communal spaces, elaborate entertainment and extravagant onboard facilities. Instead, modern premium travel increasingly revolves around privacy, personal space and individual comfort.

The upper-deck lounge remains one of the most fascinating reminders of an era when airlines were prepared to sacrifice passenger capacity in pursuit of an unforgettable flying experience.

While a handful of modern aircraft still offer onboard social spaces, the golden age of the airborne cocktail lounge is unlikely to return in its original form.

For aviation enthusiasts, however, those upstairs bars and elegant lounges will always represent a time when flying was as much about the journey as the destination.
